selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so every design choice is uncertain. Prior expectations favor multimodal, multiprofile models: RNA and image signals are likely complementary, and pooling over multiple profiles should reduce noise. 2. What it tests: This sets a strong but moderately priced baseline in the most promising region. It uses multimodal input, multiprofile avgpool aggregation, a compact scvi_n200 RNA encoder, a ResNet50 image encoder and weighted fusion. Later experiments can change one factor at a time against it: transformer aggregation, ViT-L, scGPT, concat fusion, or a single-modality ablation. 3. Why now: It starts in the likely high-accuracy region without paying for the heaviest components (ViT-L, transformer aggregation, scGPT), so it is an efficient anchor for the remaining 9 experiments. Expected cost is medium: above single-profile and single-modality runs, but well below ViT-L/transformer multimodal configurations.

1. Evidence: we have only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI, ResNet50, avgpool and weighted fusion (config_016) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1 at 5.9 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline but says nothing yet about which component limits performance. 2. Test: config_034 keeps everything the same except the image encoder, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. Because only one factor changes, any difference can be attributed to the image encoder. Pretrained image backbones are often among the biggest drivers of accuracy in cell-profiling tasks. The result tells us whether later experiments, such as aggregation, fusion and RNA-encoder variants, should build on ViT-L or ResNet50. 3. Value: this is the highest-leverage early test, combining a plausible accuracy gain with a clean ablation of a major design choice. Expected cost is higher than config_016, roughly 1.3 to 2 times or about 8 to 11 GPU hours, because ViT-L produces larger representations. The cost is justified because this choice shapes the rest of the 8-experiment budget.

1) Evidence: Two multiprofile multimodal runs share scVI RNA, avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion. Swapping the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.678 to 0.706, and F1 rose similarly. It was also cheaper (4.82 vs 5.90 GPU hours). ViT-L is therefore the current best image encoder. Aggregation is still a major untested choice: we have only tried avgpool. 2) Test: config_033 keeps the best setup (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and changes only avgpool to a transformer aggregator. This single-variable change isolates whether learned attention across multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3) Why now: it builds on the strongest result while settling a high-impact design choice early. That tells us whether later experiments, such as RNA encoder or fusion variants, should use transformer or avgpool aggregation. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_034, roughly 5 to 7 GPU hours, because of the added transformer aggregation layer. That cost is justified because this is a likely route to the top accuracy.

1) Evidence so far: ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.678 with avgpool). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706) and was also cheaper (3.6 vs 4.8 GPU h). The RNA encoder is still untested, since every run used scVI. 2) This run keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for the scGPT foundation-model encoder. It tests whether the RNA representation is a large source of accuracy gains. 3) The RNA encoder is the main design choice left unexplored, and changing it near the current best is the most informative exploit-plus-explore step. Fusion type (concat vs weighted) can be tested afterwards. Expected cost is moderate: similar to config_033 (~3.5–5 GPU h), possibly a little higher because scGPT embeddings are larger.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion), with 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Two choices look fairly well supported. ViT-L beat ResNet50 under avgpool, and transformer aggregation beat avgpool, with F1 agreeing both times. The RNA encoder matters a lot, since scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.52, so scVI is the safe choice. Fusion is still completely untested, because every run so far used weighted fusion. 2. Test: config_027 keeps the best configuration and changes only the fusion to concat. This isolates whether the fusion choice adds accuracy on top of the strongest setup. 3. Why now: Changing one variable from the current best is both the highest-value exploitation and the cleanest way to resolve an open design choice. The alternative, switching to a PCA RNA encoder (config_004), can be tested next. Expected cost is moderate and similar to config_033 (about 3.5 to 4 GPU hours). Concat may be slightly heavier than weighted fusion, but it should cost less than the avgpool and ResNet50 runs.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Across the completed runs, ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.678) and transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted and concat fusion are nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721), so fusion looks like a minor factor. RNA encoder choice has the largest effect seen so far: scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.520. The pca_n2000 encoder is still completely untested, which is the biggest remaining unknown among the main design choices. 2) This experiment swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 and keeps the best-known setup otherwise. That isolates whether PCA features can match or beat scVI. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it explores the one untested factor with large potential impact, inside the strongest known setup, so a success could directly become the new best. Whatever the result, the remaining 3 runs can then focus on refinements such as ablations or concat fusion. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3.5-5 GPU hours, similar to config_033. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add a little cost compared with the 200-dimensional scVI input.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Within multiprofile multimodal models, scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. With the image side fixed, swapping scvi (0.725) for pca_n2000 dropped accuracy to 0.586 and for scgpt to 0.520. ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.678 under avgpool). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted and concat fusion are effectively tied (0.725 vs 0.721, F1 0.685 vs 0.681). Because the RNA encoder causes such large swings, RNA appears to drive performance, but we have never measured how much the image modality actually adds. 2. What this tests: an RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer model. This is the best known setup with the image branch removed. If it matches or beats 0.725, the image branch adds little or even adds noise. That would point the last two experiments toward unimodal variants. If it falls clearly short, multimodal fusion is confirmed, and the remaining budget can go to fine-tuning around config_033, for example a single-profile or ResNet variant. 3. Why now and cost: this ablation addresses the largest remaining design uncertainty while still having a realistic chance of producing the best result. It should also be cheaper than the multimodal runs (about 3.6–5.9 GPU hours each), likely around 2–3 GPU hours, since it drops the ViT-L image branch and the fusion step.

1) Evidence: scVI RNA with the ViT-L image encoder is clearly the strongest combination so far. config_033 (transformer, weighted) leads at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1, and config_027 (transformer, concat) is close behind at 0.721. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool, ViT-L beat ResNet50, and the scGPT and PCA RNA encoders did much worse. The main design choice never tested is the profile setting: every run so far used multiprofile. 2) Test: config_042 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile, so it directly measures what multiprofile aggregation contributes. 3) Why now: the other neighbours of the best run are unpromising. ResNet50 variants such as config_025 and config_036 swap in the weaker image encoder, and avgpool variants were already worse. This run instead resolves a major untested choice. Singleprofile skips aggregation over multiple profiles, so I expect it to be cheaper than the multiprofile multimodal runs, roughly 2-3 GPU hours versus 3.6-5.9. If it competes, it opens a cheaper high-accuracy region for the final experiments; if it falls short, it confirms multiprofile with transformer aggregation as the direction to exploit.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Some choices are well supported. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT. Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted and concat fusion are about tied (0.725 vs 0.721). The image encoder is the one key choice not yet tested within the best setup. The only ResNet50 result used avgpool, where ViT-L led by about 3 points (0.706 vs 0.678). That gap may change with transformer aggregation, because the encoders could interact with how profiles are combined. 2. What this tests: config_025 changes only the image encoder relative to the best configuration (ViT-L to ResNet50, keeping scVI, transformer and weighted fusion). It shows whether ViT-L's advantage holds with transformer aggregation, or whether ResNet50 features gain more from it. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: The other options look weaker. Concat fusion is roughly tied with weighted, avgpool has already lost to transformer, and image-only or RNA-only models are unlikely to beat multimodal. This is the remaining untested single-factor change around the best configuration with a realistic chance of an improvement. Expected cost is moderate, about 4 to 6 GPU hours, similar to the earlier ResNet50 multiprofile run (5.9 h) and the other multiprofile multimodal runs.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder; PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520) did much worse. Multiprofile with transformer aggregation is consistently best. The current best is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725). ResNet50 with transformer and weighted fusion came close (0.713) and had the highest F1 so far (0.695). Concat fusion performed about the same as weighted with ViT-L (0.721 vs 0.725). 2) Test: config_036 is the only untested combination in the strongest region that changes just one factor from config_025, swapping weighted fusion for concat. It checks whether the ResNet50 + transformer setting, whose high F1 hints at headroom, can beat 0.725 under concat. 3) Why this one: with no experiments left after this, the best use is the strongest remaining exploitation candidate. The other options are weaker: avgpool variants (config_012, config_044) trailed transformer by about 2-4 points, and image-only or other encoders are unlikely to win. Expected cost is relatively high, about 5.5-6.5 GPU hours, similar to config_025. That is justified because this is the most plausible way to improve the best accuracy found.

1) Evidence: No experiments have been run, so there is no data on which modality, encoder, aggregation or fusion matters. Prior knowledge suggests multimodal, multiprofile models should do best, since they combine RNA and image signals and pool information across profiles. 2) Test: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 RNA, resnet50 image, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) is a strong but relatively cheap anchor. It checks whether the likely-best regime performs well. It uses the lighter choices on each axis: a PCA RNA encoder instead of scGPT, ResNet50 instead of ViT-L, and average pooling instead of a transformer. Later experiments can then change one axis at a time against this baseline: the aggregator (vs config_027), the encoders (scGPT/ViT-L), the fusion type (vs config_018), or dropping to unimodal or single-profile variants. 3) Why now: it should be competitive from the start while also serving as a clean reference for ablations. Expected cost is moderate: above any single-profile or unimodal run, but among the cheapest multimodal multiprofile options and well below transformer/ViT-L/scGPT variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one result exists. The multimodal multiprofile setup with PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool and weighted fusion (config_030) reached 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1 for 10.6 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline, but every design choice is still untested. 2. What this tests: config_045 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. This gives a clean single-factor comparison of the image backbone. Because the image representation often drives a large share of performance in cellular profiling, this is one of the most important open questions. 3. Why now: If ViT-L helps, it sets the backbone for later tests of aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder. If it does not help, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 for the rest of the search. Expected cost is higher than config_030, roughly 1.5 to 2 times its 10.6 GPU hours, because of the larger ViT-L representation within multiprofile multimodal training. That extra cost is justified because the backbone choice is likely to strongly affect the best reachable accuracy.

Evidence: the two completed runs share pca_n2000, avgpool and weighted fusion and differ only in image encoder. ResNet50 scored 0.639 and ViT-L 0.635 in accuracy, with F1 of 0.620 and 0.618. That gap is too small to separate them, and ViT-L was cheaper (7.0 vs 10.6 GPU hours), so I keep ViT-L as the default image encoder. Question: aggregation is the largest untested design choice in the multiprofile setting. This run keeps everything from config_045 and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation, so the change is a clean single-factor test of whether learned aggregation across profiles beats simple pooling. Why now: settling aggregation early tells us which branch to use for the remaining runs on RNA encoder (scgpt or scvi) and fusion type (concat or weighted). Expected cost is moderate, somewhat above the 7.0 GPU hours of config_045 because of the transformer aggregator, and likely still below the 10.6 hours of the ResNet50 run.

1) Evidence: avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.586 with the same pca_n2000 + ViT-L + weighted setup). This is one comparison, but the gap is large. Image encoder choice matters little: ResNet50 scored 0.639 and ViT-L 0.635, a difference within noise, and ViT-L was cheaper (7.0 vs 10.6 GPU h). The RNA encoder has never been varied; every run so far used pca_n2000. 2) This experiment keeps the best known backbone (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion, ViT-L) and swaps pca_n2000 for scGPT. It isolates whether a pretrained RNA foundation embedding beats PCA features. 3) The RNA encoder is the largest untested design choice and could move accuracy more than the small image-encoder difference. Fixing the other choices at their best known values means the result directly guides the remaining 6 experiments, for example whether to try scVI next or switch to tuning fusion. scvi_n200 (config_041) would be the cheaper way to test the RNA encoder, but I chose scGPT because I expect it is the more likely of the two to beat PCA. Expected cost: moderate, roughly similar to config_045 (~7–9 GPU h). It is cheaper than the ResNet50 variant, though scGPT embeddings may add some overhead.

1) Evidence so far: among multiprofile multimodal runs, the RNA encoder has the largest observed effect. pca_n2000 reached about 0.635-0.639, while scgpt reached 0.542 under otherwise identical settings. avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.586). ResNet50 and ViT-L are close (0.639 vs 0.635), and the ViT-L run cost less (7.0 vs 10.6 GPU h). The third RNA encoder, scvi_n200, is still untested, and so is concat fusion. 2) This run swaps only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200 in the config_045 setup (ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion). Because one factor changes, it shows directly whether scvi can match or beat pca_n2000 on the factor that has mattered most. 3) It is the best use of the next slot because an untested RNA encoder carries the largest remaining uncertainty and potential upside, given how strongly this factor has moved accuracy. The concat-versus-weighted fusion question can follow on the winning encoder. Expected cost is relatively low, roughly at or below config_045's 7 GPU h, since scvi's 200-dimensional input is smaller than PCA's 2000 and ViT-L has been cheaper here than ResNet50.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the strongest factor so far. scvi_n200 reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1, compared with about 0.635 for pca_n2000 and 0.542 for scGPT, all with ViT-L, avgpool and weighted fusion. Avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.586). ViT-L and ResNet50 performed about the same with PCA, and ViT-L was cheaper (7.0 vs 10.6 GPU h). Fusion has never been varied: every run used weighted fusion, so it is the main untested design choice. 2) Test: this keeps the best configuration fixed (scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool) and changes only weighted to concat fusion. That isolates whether concat can raise accuracy above 0.706. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while settling an open design choice, which leaves 3 runs for follow-ups such as the ResNet50 or single-profile variants of the winner. Expected cost is moderate, similar to config_041 (about 5 GPU h). That is well below the ResNet50 multiprofile runs and in line with the cheaper ViT-L configurations.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reached 0.706 to 0.715 accuracy, while pca_n2000 reached about 0.635 to 0.639 and scgpt reached 0.542. Avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.586 with pca). Concat fusion was slightly better than weighted with scvi (0.715 vs 0.706, F1 0.687 vs 0.667). The image encoder is the main open question. With pca, ResNet50 and ViT-L performed about the same (0.639 vs 0.635), but that comparison came from a weaker RNA backbone, so it may not carry over to scvi. 2) Test: config_020 keeps every part of the best configuration (config_046: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50. This is a clean one-variable comparison that shows whether ResNet50 image features add more to the strong scvi representation. 3) Why now: it directly exploits the best region while closing the last untested axis that could plausibly beat 0.715. Transformer aggregation already looks harmful, so it is a poorer use of a run. Expected cost is moderate to high, roughly 1.5 to 2 times config_046 (about 7 to 10 GPU hours), since the earlier ResNet50 run cost more than its ViT-L counterpart. That is still acceptable given 3 runs remain and the potential accuracy gain.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.706 and 0.715, versus 0.635 to 0.639 for pca and 0.542 for scgpt). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 with scvi (0.715 vs 0.632). Concat fusion is slightly ahead of weighted (0.715 vs 0.706, also better F1). Transformer aggregation hurt badly in the one test with pca (0.586 vs 0.635), so transformer variants are unpromising. The main untested dimension is the profile setting: all 7 runs used multiprofile. 2) Test: config_017 keeps the best components (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + concat) and switches to singleprofile. This shows whether multiprofile avgpool aggregation actually helps or whether a simpler single-profile model matches or beats it. 3) Why now: it isolates one important design choice next to the current best (config_046). It should also be cheaper than the multiprofile runs (about 4.5 to 4.8 GPU h), likely about 2 to 3 GPU h, since it has no multiprofile aggregation. If it wins, the last 2 experiments can refine singleprofile variants; if it loses, multiprofile is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to small refinements such as an RNA-only check.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT (0.706–0.715 vs ≤0.639). ViT-L also clearly beats ResNet50 when paired with scVI (0.715 vs 0.632). Concat fusion is slightly better than weighted (0.715 vs 0.706, with higher F1, 0.687 vs 0.667). The best result is config_046 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat). The main open design choice for this best pairing is aggregation. Transformer aggregation was tested only once, with PCA + ViT-L + weighted, where it dropped accuracy (0.586 vs 0.635). One run with a weaker RNA encoder is not strong evidence that a transformer cannot help with the richer scVI embeddings. 2) This experiment: config_034 changes only the aggregation of the current best configuration, from avgpool to transformer. It directly tests whether learned attention over multiple profiles can improve on mean pooling for the strongest encoder pair. 3) Why now: it is the only untested logical neighbour of the best configuration that keeps all the clearly winning choices (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, concat). Unimodal or single-profile options are unlikely to beat 0.715, given that single-profile scored 0.532. Expected cost is moderate, about 4–5 GPU hours, similar to config_046. Transformer runs have so far trained no slower than avgpool, so it is cheaper than any ResNet or PCA configuration. If it underperforms, the final experiment can still exploit around config_046.

1) Evidence: scVI-200 RNA plus ViT-L images, multiprofile, is clearly the strongest region, at 0.706–0.721. Swapping in ResNet50, PCA or scGPT drops accuracy sharply. The best result so far is config_034 (transformer, concat) at 0.7207. Within scVI/ViT-L, concat beat weighted only slightly under avgpool (0.715 vs 0.706), and transformer slightly beat avgpool under concat. Weighted fusion has never been tested with scVI and transformer aggregation together. 2) This experiment completes the scVI/ViT-L aggregation × fusion grid. It tests whether weighted fusion pairs better with transformer aggregation than with avgpool, which is the last close neighbour of the best configuration. 3) As the final experiment, the best use of budget is exploiting the best region rather than speculative exploration. RNA-only, image-only and ResNet50/scGPT variants have weak prospects given the strong ViT-L and scVI effects seen so far. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to the other scVI/ViT-L multiprofile runs and cheaper than the ResNet50 or PCA variants.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been completed, so every design choice is uncertain. Prior expectations from multimodal cellular profiling suggest that combining RNA and image signals, and aggregating across multiple profiles, are the choices most likely to give high accuracy. 2) Test: config_004 is a strong, representative anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, uses a compact scVI (200-dim) RNA encoder and a strong ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, with simple avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. It tests whether the likely-best regime (multimodal plus multiprofile) performs well before any finer choices are tuned. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time from this baseline: transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, the RNA encoder, or single-modality controls. 3) Why now: it is a high-prior candidate for the top accuracy and still controls cost. Expected cost is moderate: higher than single-profile or unimodal runs because of multiprofile, multimodal processing and ViT-L features, but cheaper than transformer-aggregation variants or larger RNA representations such as PCA-2000 or scGPT.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1 for 4.49 GPU hours. That is a reasonable baseline, but it says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_041 changes only one factor, replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation. Because everything else is held fixed, the result isolates whether learned attention over profiles beats simple mean pooling. This is a major architectural choice and plausibly the biggest lever for accuracy in a multiprofile setup. 3) Why now: a clean one-factor comparison against the strong baseline either opens a better direction to exploit or rules it out early. Encoder and fusion comparisons can follow with the 8 remaining experiments. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_004, perhaps about 1.2 to 1.5 times its cost (about 5.5 to 7 GPU hours), because transformer aggregation over multiple profiles with ViT-L features adds compute. The potential gain justifies this.

1. Evidence so far: the two runs share scvi_n200, ViT-L and concat fusion and differ only in aggregation. Transformer reached 0.7207 accuracy versus 0.7150 for avgpool, but its F1 was slightly lower (0.681 vs 0.687). Aggregation therefore looks like a minor factor, and the bigger untested choices are the RNA encoder, the image encoder and the fusion type. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps the current best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to the scGPT foundation-model embeddings. This isolates whether RNA representation quality is a major lever, which is plausible since it carries much of the biological signal. 3. Why now: a one-variable change from the best config gives a clean attribution, and with 7 runs left, settling the RNA encoder early guides the rest of the search. Expected cost is similar to or slightly above the previous runs, about 4.7–5 GPU hours, because scGPT embeddings may be somewhat larger than scvi_n200.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt dropped accuracy from about 0.72 to 0.51. Aggregation matters little: transformer scored 0.721 and avgpool 0.715, a gap too small to rely on, and avgpool had slightly higher F1. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is still untested, and so are weighted fusion and resnet50. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. That isolates the factor with the largest observed effect and shows whether a higher-dimensional linear RNA representation beats scVI. 3) Why now: with 6 experiments left, resolving the highest-impact open choice first tells us which RNA encoder to build on for later fusion and image-encoder tests, and it could directly produce a new best. Expected cost is similar to the prior multiprofile ViT-L transformer runs, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more because of the 2000-dimensional RNA input.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reaches about 0.715 to 0.721 accuracy, far above pca_n2000 (0.599) and scgpt (0.507). Transformer and avgpool aggregation perform almost the same with scvi_n200 (0.721 vs 0.715, and avgpool has slightly higher F1), so aggregation looks like a minor factor. Two design choices remain completely untested: fusion type (only concat has been tried) and image encoder (only imagenet_vit_l has been tried). 2. Test: config_050 keeps the current best setup (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This cleanly isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest base. 3. Why now: Fusion directly controls how the two modalities are combined, so it is a plausible lever for beating 0.72. A one-variable change from the best configuration both exploits that configuration and resolves a key uncertainty. The result will tell us whether later experiments should use weighted fusion. Testing resnet50 (for example config_006) is a cheaper follow-up for the image-encoder question. Expected cost is similar to config_041, roughly 4.5 to 4.8 GPU hours, which is among the more expensive options but justified because this is the most likely path to a new best.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder so far, at about 0.715-0.725 accuracy versus 0.60 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT. Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion each gave small gains, and the current best is config_050 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy. Every run so far used ViT-L as the image encoder, so whether the image backbone matters is still unknown. 2) This run keeps the best recipe and swaps only ViT-L for ResNet50. That isolates the effect of the image encoder: it will show whether the larger ViT-L is necessary or whether a lighter CNN backbone matches or beats it. 3) It is the best use of the budget because it settles the last major untested design choice while staying in the best-performing region. It is also likely cheaper than config_050's 3.6 GPU hours, since ResNet50 is a smaller backbone with smaller representations. Expected relative cost is low to moderate. If it performs as well, later runs can use the cheaper backbone; if it does worse, ViT-L is confirmed and the remaining runs can refine aggregation and fusion around config_050.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (~0.72 versus 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). ImageNet ViT-L slightly beats ResNet50 on accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713) and trained cheaper here (3.60 vs 6.22 GPU h). Weighted fusion edged out concat with transformer aggregation (0.725 vs 0.721). Transformer edged out avgpool under concat (0.721 vs 0.715), but these gaps are small, so the aggregation choice remains uncertain. 2) Test: config_019 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) is the one missing cell of the 2x2 aggregation x fusion grid around the current best, config_050. It shows whether weighted fusion also helps avgpool and whether the cheaper avgpool aggregator can match or beat transformer. 3) Why now: this exploits the strongest region of the space with a low-risk local variation that could set a new best, and it sharpens the aggregation decision for the last experiments. Expected cost is moderate and similar to or slightly below the transformer runs, roughly 3.5-4.5 GPU hours, cheaper than the ResNet50 variants.

1) Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder is clearly the most important choice so far (about 0.71-0.725, versus 0.60 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT). Within scVI + ViT-L multiprofile, all four aggregation/fusion combinations are now tested. The best is transformer + weighted fusion (config_050, 0.725), and the differences among the four are small (0.706-0.725). Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 gave slightly lower accuracy (0.713), though with slightly higher F1, at higher cost. The largest untested design choice is the profile setting: every run so far was multiprofile. 2) Test: config_009 keeps the strongest components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) but switches to singleprofile. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed or whether a simpler setup matches or beats it. 3) Rationale: the remaining multiprofile scVI variants (such as ResNet50 with concat or avgpool) are expected to give only marginal changes, given the small differences seen so far and ResNet's higher cost. This experiment instead resolves real uncertainty about a major untested factor, and the result will guide the final two experiments. Expected cost is low relative to prior runs, likely about 2-3 GPU hours, since there is no multiprofile aggregation.

Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. With the same multiprofile ViT-L transformer setup, scvi_n200 scored about 0.72, pca_n2000 0.60 and scgpt 0.51. Multiprofile aggregation is also essential, since the single-profile run reached only 0.54. Fusion, aggregation and image-encoder changes moved accuracy by only about 0.01 (the best is config_050 at 0.725). The best result so far is config_018 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool with this setup (0.725 vs 0.706), and its F1 was also higher. ViT-L and ResNet50 were close (0.725 vs 0.713), and ViT-L was cheaper. The fusion method is the one major design choice never tested: every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) This experiment: config_042 keeps the best setup and changes only fusion to concat. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.71-0.725 vs 0.52 for scgpt and 0.59 for pca). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy, 3.6 GPU h). 1. Evidence: The strongest region is clear. scVI beats pca_n2000 by about 0.14 and scGPT by about 0.20. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by about 0.019. Multiprofile beats singleprofile by about 0.19, and multimodal beats RNA-only by about 0.07. Within this region, the best result is config_018 (ViT-L, weighted, 0.725). The neighbouring configs config_042 (ViT-L, concat, 0.721) and config_003 (ResNet50, weighted, 0.713) score within about 0.012 of it. Those gaps are small enough to fall within run-to-run noise. 2. What it tests: config_033 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + concat) is the only untested scVI/transformer/multiprofile multimodal combination. It completes the image-encoder by fusion comparison, showing whether ResNet50 pairs better with concat fusion than with weighted fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of the slot: every other remaining option drops at least one component that clearly helped. Those are either scGPT or PCA instead of scVI, avgpool instead of transformer, singleprofile, or a single modality, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This makes config_033 the highest-probability, if modest, chance of a new best. Expected cost is relatively high, around 5-6 GPU hours, similar to config_003 (6.22 h). 1) Evidence: the strongest region is clear. It is multimodal, multiprofile, with an scVI-n200 RNA encoder and an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder. The best run is config_018 (transformer, weighted) at 0.725, followed by config_042 (concat) at 0.721 and config_016 (avgpool) at 0.706. Swapping in scGPT or PCA for RNA dropped accuracy sharply (0.52–0.59). Single-profile and RNA-only runs were also clearly worse, and ResNet50 is slightly behind ViT-L. 2) This experiment: config_007 is the only untested scVI + ViT-L multiprofile combination left. It tests avgpool aggregation together with concat fusion. Image-only or other-encoder options have weak or negative evidence, and the remaining scVI + ResNet50 avgpool variants pair the weaker image encoder with the weaker aggregation. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. These choices are modality, single vs. multiple profiles, RNA and image encoder, aggregation and fusion. Prior expectation is that combining both modalities and aggregating multiple profiles should give the strongest signal, but this is unconfirmed here. 2. What it tests: config_001 is a multimodal, multiprofile setup built from the cheaper components: scVI-200 RNA embeddings, a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and simple concat fusion. Its accuracy will show whether the multimodal + multiprofile direction is promising before paying for more expensive parts. 3. Why now: It is a mid-cost anchor that later experiments can compare against by changing one factor at a time. Candidate swaps include ViT-L for ResNet50, transformer for avgpool, weighted for concat, scGPT or PCA for scVI, and single-modality ablations. This leaves 9 experiments to exploit what it reveals. Expected relative cost: moderate. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_001 (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1 at 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline in what is probably the strongest region of the space, but every design axis is still untested. 2) Test: config_049 changes exactly one factor, swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation. Any difference can therefore be attributed to how the multiple profiles are combined. A learned, attention-based aggregator could plausibly beat mean pooling, while the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion choices stay fixed. 3) Why now: aggregation is likely a high-impact choice that affects many of the remaining multiprofile configurations, so settling it early guides much of the remaining 8-experiment budget. Swapping in the ViT-L image encoder instead would likely cost more. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_001 because of the transformer aggregator, roughly 8-10 GPU hours, which is less than the larger-encoder alternatives.

Evidence: with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat), transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool on both accuracy (0.688 vs 0.632) and F1 (0.659 vs 0.607). It was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU h), so transformer aggregation is the current anchor. The image encoder is still untested and is a high-impact choice, since ViT-L representations are much richer than ResNet50. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_049) and changes only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. That cleanly measures the encoder's effect and exploits the strongest known direction. It is the best use of a limited budget because the encoder choice likely moves accuracy more than fusion type, and the answer shapes most of the remaining search. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_049, roughly 1.3-1.8x, because ViT-L features are larger, though transformer aggregation should keep it under about 8 GPU h. If the gain is small, later experiments can return to cheaper ResNet50 variants such as weighted fusion or scGPT.

1) Evidence: with the scVI RNA encoder and concat fusion fixed, transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L under transformer aggregation raised accuracy to 0.721 (F1 0.681), the current best (config_018). Fusion has never been varied: every run used concat. The RNA encoder alternatives (PCA, scGPT) are also untested. 2) Test: config_007 matches the best configuration except for weighted fusion instead of concat. This one-factor change isolates the effect of fusion on top of the strongest setup, and F1 can confirm whether any gain is real. 3) Why now: it directly exploits the best configuration found so far while resolving an unexplored design choice that affects every future multimodal candidate. Weighted fusion only adds learned modality weights to the same encoders, so I expect it to cost about the same as config_018 (roughly 4.5-5.5 GPU hours). That is cheaper than the avgpool baseline run and no more expensive than switching to a heavier encoder such as scGPT, which can be tested next on whichever fusion wins.

1. Evidence: Every run so far uses the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Three image/aggregation/fusion choices have clear evidence. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (0.688 vs 0.632). ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3.3 points (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion edged out concat (0.725 vs 0.721, with F1 also slightly higher), though that gap is small. The biggest untested axis is the RNA encoder. 2. Test: config_024 keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps in scGPT. Changing only one factor isolates whether a pretrained single-cell foundation model improves the RNA representation over scvi_n200. 3. Why now: this extends the strongest direction while reducing uncertainty on the main open design choice. If scGPT helps, the remaining budget can refine around it. If it does not, pca_n2000 (config_005) is the natural next comparison. 1) Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion is slightly ahead of concat (0.725 vs 0.721), a small difference. Swapping the RNA encoder to scgpt in the best setup collapsed accuracy to 0.520, so the RNA encoder is a high-impact choice. pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2) config_005 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This shows whether scvi_n200 is truly the best RNA representation or whether a higher-dimensional PCA input does better. 3) It is the factor with the largest remaining uncertainty and a plausible chance of a new best result, while staying in the strongest region of the search space. 1) Evidence: every run so far has used multiprofile. The best result is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.06, ViT-L beat ResNet50, and weighted fusion was slightly ahead of concat. scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder, well ahead of PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520). 2) Untested choice: whether to aggregate across multiple profiles at all. This run keeps the strongest components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile, which directly tests that axis. avgpool variants such as config_012 are unlikely to win given the earlier aggregation gap. 3) Why now: single-profile models skip the costly aggregation step, so this should be the cheapest multimodal run yet, likely below the roughly 3.6 to 4.7 GPU hours of earlier ViT-L runs. If it matches or beats config_007, the last runs can focus on cheaper single-profile variants. If it falls short, it confirms multiprofile with transformer as the backbone, and I would use the final runs to test image-only and RNA-only references (configs 029 and 040).

Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Within this neighbourhood, scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA, ViT-L beats ResNet50, and weighted fusion edges concat by a small margin. The weakest-tested choice in the top region is aggregation. Transformer beat avgpool only once, with ResNet50 and concat fusion (0.688 vs 0.632), and avgpool was never tried with ViT-L features. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). Its close neighbours scored slightly lower: concat fusion gave 0.721 and avgpool aggregation gave 0.706. Switching to ResNet50 cost about 0.03 and multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. So the remaining multimodal variants (config_044, config_026) are likely to land around 0.69 to 0.71 and unlikely to beat the best. The main untested question is how much each modality contributes. Swapping scVI for scGPT or PCA cut accuracy sharply (0.52 and 0.59), and weighted fusion did not protect against this. That shows the RNA branch strongly shapes results, but we still do not know whether a ViT-L image-only model is competitive. 2) This experiment tests image-only ViT-L with multiprofile transformer aggregation, the strongest image-side setup. 1) Evidence: the best result is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The remaining multimodal neighbours of the best config look unlikely to beat it, since each swaps in a component that has already underperformed (e.g., config_044 uses ResNet50, config_026 uses avgpool). 1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence and uncertainty covers every design axis. Priors from multimodal cell profiling suggest that combining RNA and image signals, and aggregating several profiles per sample, usually gives the highest accuracy. 2. What this tests: it sets a strong anchor for the likely best region of the search space, a multimodal multiprofile model. It uses a compact, well-regularized RNA embedding (scVI, 200 dimensions), a strong image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L), weighted fusion and simple average pooling. Later runs can change one factor at a time against this anchor: transformer versus avgpool aggregation, scGPT or PCA versus scVI, ResNet50 versus ViT-L, single versus multiple profiles, and unimodal ablations. 3. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1 for 4.82 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable anchor, but we know nothing yet about which design choices drive performance. 2. What this tests: config_050 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. Why it is the best next step: a single-variable change gives a clean answer that will guide the remaining 8 experiments. A transformer aggregator is also a plausible route to beating the baseline. 1) Evidence: the only aggregation comparison so far favors the transformer over avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706 accuracy, 0.685 vs 0.667 F1), with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted fusion). The transformer run was also cheaper (3.6 vs 4.8 GPU hours). So I will keep the transformer. 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder so far. Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. Changing fusion (concat) or the image encoder (ResNet50) moved accuracy only about 0.005-0.012, and those differences are too small to read much into. Uncertainty: since the RNA encoder drives most of the variation, it is unclear whether the image branch adds anything on top of scVI. If it matches or beats the multimodal models, it points the last two experiments toward RNA-centric variants. If it falls short, it confirms that the image modality contributes and that refining multimodal fusion is worthwhile. 1) Evidence: scVI RNA with multiprofile transformer aggregation is clearly the strongest family. It produced the best result so far, config_050 (ViT-L, weighted, 0.725). 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 at 0.725 accuracy (scVI-n200 RNA, ViT-L images, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). Test: config_024 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a learned transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. Any change in accuracy can therefore be attributed to aggregation. Evidence: across three multimodal multiprofile runs, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l added about 3.3 more points, giving the current best, config_025 at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Fusion is the one design choice not yet tested at all, since every run so far used concat. This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer) and changes only fusion to weighted. That isolates whether learned modality weighting improves on concatenation. It is a direct one-factor extension of the strongest configuration, so it both exploits the best region and settles a design choice that affects every later multimodal candidate. Once fusion is settled, the RNA encoder (scgpt or pca) can be tested next with the better fusion. Expected cost is similar to config_025, roughly 4.5–5.5 GPU hours, because weighted fusion adds little over concat. That is cheaper than the avgpool runs measured so far.

Evidence: across four multiprofile multimodal runs, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (config_024 vs config_038, both scVI+ResNet50+concat). ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3.3 points (config_025 vs config_024). Weighted fusion edged out concat by about 0.4 points (config_035 vs config_025), with a matching F1 gain, though that gap is small. The RNA encoder is the main design choice still untested: every run so far used scvi_n200. This experiment keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for the scGPT foundation-model embeddings. It isolates the RNA encoder effect, which is the most plausible remaining source of a sizeable gain. It is the best use of the next slot because it exploits the established best direction while closing the largest gap in our knowledge. Whatever the result, it tells us which RNA encoder to carry through the remaining four experiments; PCA can be checked later if scGPT does not help. Expected cost is moderate, similar to the other transformer ViT-L runs (about 4–5 GPU hours), possibly slightly more because scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted fusion), with 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). ViT-L beat resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion was slightly better than concat, but the gap is too small to rely on. Swapping in scGPT as the RNA encoder caused a large drop (0.520). The main open question is the RNA encoder: pca_n2000 has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the strongest image encoder, aggregation and fusion settings and swaps in pca_n2000. It directly tests whether a higher-dimensional PCA RNA representation can beat scVI within the best architecture. 3) This is the most informative remaining design choice that could still raise the best accuracy, and it builds on strong existing evidence. Expected cost is moderate, about 4 to 5 GPU hours. That is similar to config_025 and config_035, perhaps slightly more because of the 2000-dimensional RNA input, and well below the avgpool/resnet50 run (7.27 h).

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1), with config_025 (concat fusion) close behind. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). ViT-L beats ResNet50. Weighted and concat fusion are roughly equal. The RNA encoder matters a great deal: swapping scVI for scGPT (0.520) or PCA (0.586) causes large drops. The most important open question is whether the RNA branch adds value at all, or whether the image pathway (ViT-L + transformer) is doing most of the work. Weak RNA encoders appear to actively harm the model. 2) This experiment: image-only multiprofile ViT-L with transformer aggregation isolates the strongest image pathway. If it matches or exceeds about 0.72, multimodal fusion is not essential, and the remaining budget should shift to image-centric variants. If it falls clearly below, scVI-based fusion is confirmed as the main driver, and the last runs can refine around config_035. 3) Why now: the remaining near-best multimodal variants mostly swap in components already shown to be inferior (avgpool in config_029, ResNet50 in config_042), so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This run resolves the largest remaining design uncertainty (modality contribution) and has a plausible chance of being competitive. Expected cost is low to moderate, likely below the roughly 3.6–4.7 GPU hours of the multimodal ViT-L transformer runs, because there is no RNA encoder or fusion.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy). Each single-factor change from it has been worse. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT gave 0.520 and to PCA gave 0.586. Switching the image encoder to ResNet50 (in the concat setting) cost about 0.03. Using avgpool instead of transformer aggregation cost about 0.056. Image-only performance is very poor (0.260), and weighted fusion edging out concat hints that the model may be down-weighting the image branch. 2) What this tests: the remaining single-swap neighbours of the best config look unlikely to beat it. ResNet50 + weighted (config_042) would be expected near 0.69, and ViT-L + avgpool (config_029) near 0.67. The largest open question is therefore how much the image modality actually contributes. config_032 keeps the winning scVI encoder and transformer aggregation but drops the image branch. If it matches or beats 0.725, the last run should focus on RNA-centric variants. If it falls clearly below, image fusion is confirmed as useful and the final run can refine the multimodal configuration. 3) Why now and cost: it resolves a key design question that no other experiment addresses and has some chance of matching the best result. Without an image encoder it should be among the cheapest runs, likely about 1–2 GPU hours, similar to the 1.44 h image-only run and well below the 3.6–7.3 h multimodal runs.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Within this space the evidence is fairly consistent: scVI beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer aggregation beats avgpool (+0.056 with ResNet50), and weighted fusion is slightly better than concat. The remaining untested multiprofile neighbours of the best config each change one of these choices in the direction that has lost so far. config_042 swaps in ResNet50 (expected about 0.69), and config_029 or config_007 swap in avgpool (expected about 0.66–0.67). So they are unlikely to beat 0.725. The one major design choice never tested is single-profile versus multiprofile input. 2. Test: config_014 keeps the best components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) but uses single-profile input with no aggregation. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed or whether a simpler setup does as well or better. 3. Why now: Among the options, this is the one with real uncertainty and a plausible chance of exceeding 0.725, rather than a near-certain loss. If it does well, it also points the final experiment toward single-profile variants. Expected cost is low: with no multiprofile aggregation it should be cheaper than the roughly 3.6–4.7 GPU-hour multiprofile ViT-L runs, likely around 2 GPU hours or less.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Three choices are consistently strong: the scVI RNA encoder (clearly ahead of scGPT and PCA), transformer aggregation (about 0.056 better than avgpool on ResNet50), and multimodal fusion (ahead of RNA-only at 0.653 and image-only at 0.260). Weighted fusion beat concat only slightly (0.725 vs 0.721). The one untested combination within this scVI + transformer family is ResNet50 with weighted fusion. This experiment tests whether the weighted-fusion gain carries over to ResNet50, which scored 0.688 with concat. That would show whether the image encoder and the fusion choice interact. With no budget left, a nearby variant of the strongest family is a better final bet than avgpool variants such as config_029, which history suggests will underperform. It is also better than PCA or scGPT variants, which have done poorly. Winning outright is unlikely, since ResNet50 has trailed ViT-L, so config_035 will probably stay the best. Expected cost is moderate, about 4–5 GPU hours, similar to config_024.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no data on any design choice. Domain priors suggest that multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation with a learned (transformer) aggregator are the most likely to give high accuracy. Which RNA encoder and image encoder work best is still the largest open question. 2) What this tests: config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) is a strong-prior, near-full-capacity baseline. Its result anchors the search. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: ViT-L vs ResNet50, scGPT/PCA vs scVI, avgpool vs transformer, concat vs weighted, and unimodal ablations. 3) Why now: starting from a likely-good configuration gives a competitive incumbent early, which protects the best-found accuracy, while keeping compute moderate. Expected relative cost is medium. Multiprofile aggregation plus a transformer and two modalities add cost. The compact 200-dimensional scVI embedding and the ResNet50 backbone keep it well below the ViT-L or scGPT multiprofile variants.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1 at 6.22 GPU hours. That is a reasonable anchor, but one run tells us nothing about which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_046 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. This isolates the effect of the image representation, which may be one of the highest-impact factors for multimodal accuracy. 3. Why now: a one-factor change from a known anchor gives a clean, interpretable result. If ViT-L clearly helps, later experiments can tune the RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion on top of it. If it does not, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 backbone. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_019, perhaps about 1.3 to 1.8 times, because the ViT-L features are larger. This is justified because the image encoder could be the deciding factor for the best accuracy.

1. Evidence: Two multiprofile, transformer, weighted-fusion runs differ only in the image encoder. ImageNet ViT-L reached higher accuracy than ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.713) and used much less compute (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h), though its F1 was slightly lower. That gives a tentative lead to ViT-L, but the RNA encoder, fusion and aggregation choices are still completely untested. 2. Test: This run keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps scVI-200 for scGPT. It isolates the RNA encoder, which is a major design axis likely to shift accuracy more than fusion or aggregation details. 3. Why now: Testing the RNA encoder exploits the promising ViT-L direction while reducing a key uncertainty early, so the remaining budget can be focused on the better RNA backbone before tuning fusion (concat) and aggregation (avgpool). Expected cost is moderate, similar to or slightly above config_046 (about 3.5-5 GPU h), and well below the ResNet50 run.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder has had the largest effect so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt, with everything else held fixed, dropped validation accuracy from 0.725 to 0.520. The image encoder mattered much less. imagenet_vit_l scored 0.725 against 0.713 for resnet50, a small gap, and was cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU hours), though resnet50 had slightly higher F1. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is still untested. It could plausibly match or beat scvi. 2. Test: config_035 keeps the current best setup (vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This is a clean one-factor comparison with config_046 and config_002. 3. Why now: Because the RNA encoder has shown the highest impact, settling it should come before tuning smaller factors like fusion (concat vs weighted) or aggregation (avgpool vs transformer). Those can be tuned on the winning encoder in the remaining 6 experiments. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3-4 GPU hours, similar to config_046. PCA features are cheap, and vit_l runs have so far been cheaper than resnet50 runs.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (about 0.71-0.72 accuracy, versus 0.59 for pca_n2000 and 0.52 for scgpt). With scvi, imagenet_vit_l gave slightly higher accuracy than resnet50 (0.725 vs 0.713) and was cheaper to train (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h). That makes config_046 the current best and the cheaper base to build on. 2) Uncertainty: every run so far used weighted fusion with transformer aggregation, so the fusion choice is completely untested. config_039 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer) and changes only fusion to concat. This isolates the effect of fusion and could beat 0.725. 3) Why now: it is a one-factor change around the best configuration, so it directly exploits the strong evidence while clarifying an untested design choice. The aggregation question (avgpool, config_001) can follow in the remaining budget. Expected cost is similar to config_046, about 3.5-4 GPU hours, since concat fusion adds little overhead.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder. It reached 0.713 to 0.725, while scgpt reached 0.52 and pca_n2000 reached 0.59. With scvi, imagenet_vit_l slightly beat resnet50 (0.725 vs 0.713) and cost less. Weighted and concat fusion were nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721, F1 0.685 vs 0.681). Every run so far used transformer aggregation, so the aggregation choice is still completely unknown. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. That isolates whether a simpler aggregator matches or beats the transformer. 3) It is the most informative remaining test around the current best region, and it could improve the top accuracy. Expected cost is at or below config_046's 3.6 GPU hours, since avgpool is cheaper than transformer aggregation. That makes it a low-cost test of a high-value design choice.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_046 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725. Changing the RNA encoder moved accuracy a lot: scVI reached about 0.71-0.72, PCA 0.586 and scGPT 0.520. Changing the image encoder (ResNet50 0.713 vs ViT-L 0.725), the fusion method (concat 0.721) or the aggregation (avgpool 0.706) moved it much less. So the RNA branch seems to drive performance, and it is unclear how much the image branch adds. The remaining multimodal scVI variants (ResNet50 or avgpool with concat) look unlikely to beat 0.725, given their components each tested lower. 2. Test: config_022 is the RNA-only scVI model with the transformer aggregator. It shows whether the image branch genuinely helps or mostly adds noise and compute. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.725, it becomes the new best and points the last experiments toward RNA-centric variants. If it falls clearly short, that confirms multimodal fusion matters and the remaining budget should refine around config_046. 3. Why now: it resolves the biggest open design question (modality) using the strongest RNA encoder and the best aggregator. It is also likely cheaper than the multimodal runs (estimated about 2-3 GPU hours versus 3.6-6.2) because there is no image encoder or fusion step.

Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. It scored 0.70-0.725, compared with 0.52 for scGPT and 0.59 for PCA. Within scVI multimodal runs, the transformer beat avgpool, ViT-L beat ResNet50, and weighted fusion edged out concat (0.725 vs 0.721, also with slightly higher F1). The best so far is config_046 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted). The remaining scVI multiprofile variants (e.g. ResNet50+concat, avgpool+concat) combine choices that each scored lower, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. The main unexplored design axis is the profile setting: every run so far used multiprofile. Test: config_040 is config_046 with singleprofile instead of multiprofile (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion, no aggregation). It isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps. Why now: with 2 experiments left, this resolves the largest remaining uncertainty and has some chance of a surprise improvement. If singleprofile proves competitive, the last run can exploit it, for example with concat fusion. Expected cost is low, likely below config_046's 3.6 GPU hours, because no multiprofile aggregation is involved.

1. Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder with multiprofile transformer aggregation is clearly the strongest family. config_046 (ViT-L, weighted) is best at 0.725, config_039 (ViT-L, concat) reached 0.721 and config_019 (ResNet50, weighted) reached 0.713. Switching to scGPT or PCA RNA encoders, avgpool aggregation, single-profile input or RNA-only all lowered accuracy substantially. 2. Test: config_031 (scVI, ResNet50, transformer, concat) is the only untested combination in this top family. It checks whether concat fusion helps the ResNet50 image encoder, since the fusion choices differed by only about 0.004 accuracy with ViT-L. 3. Why now: every remaining alternative relies on a choice that has already hurt performance, such as avgpool, a weaker RNA encoder or dropping a modality. config_031 is therefore the most plausible remaining chance to match or slightly beat 0.725, although I expect it to land around 0.71 to 0.72, so a gain is uncertain. Expected cost is relatively high, about 5–6 GPU hours, similar to config_019 (6.22 GPU hours) because of ResNet50 multiprofile multimodal processing. I accept this cost because no cheaper configuration has a realistic chance of beating the current best.

1. Evidence: The scVI-n200 RNA encoder with the ViT-L image encoder under multiprofile aggregation is clearly the strongest region. Results so far are config_046 (transformer, weighted) at 0.725, config_039 (transformer, concat) at 0.721 and config_001 (avgpool, weighted) at 0.706. ResNet50 trails ViT-L by about 0.01–0.03. scGPT and PCA RNA encoders, single-profile and RNA-only models all perform much worse. Every scVI + ViT-L + multiprofile configuration except avgpool with concat has already been tested. 2. This run tests that last cell (avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and checks whether concat interacts better with avgpool than weighted fusion did. 3. Why it is the best final pick: it is the only untested configuration in the top-performing region, so it has the highest remaining chance of matching or beating 0.725. The alternatives are weaker. ResNet50 avgpool variants (config_011, config_032) start from a weaker image encoder. Image-only models dropped the RNA signal that multimodal runs relied on. Any scGPT or PCA run is likely to score well below the best. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_001 and config_039 and cheaper than the ResNet50 transformer runs.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run yet, so every design choice is open: modality, profile setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. Prior expectation is that multimodal multiprofile models perform best in cellular profiling, but neither that nor the relative cost of each choice has been measured. 2) What this tests: config_020 sets a mid-complexity multimodal multiprofile anchor using scVI (200-dim), ResNet50, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. These are moderate, commonly strong defaults. Later runs can change one factor at a time against this baseline (transformer aggregation, ViT-L image encoder, weighted fusion, single-modality ablations) to attribute gains to specific components. 3) Why now: it likely sits in the high-accuracy region (multimodal plus multiprofile), which helps the best-found objective. It also avoids starting with the most expensive options (ViT-L with transformer aggregation) before knowing whether that cost pays off. Expected relative cost: moderate. Multiprofile and multimodal add cost, but the compact scVI latent, ResNet50 and avgpool keep it well below ViT-L/transformer configurations.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result. The multimodal, multiprofile config_020 (scVI RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. No design choice has been compared yet. 2. What this tests: config_003 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else the same. Any difference can therefore be credited cleanly to the image encoder, which is likely one of the most influential choices. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: larger pretrained ViT image features often improve morphology representations, so this has a good chance of raising the best accuracy. It also settles an encoder choice that later experiments can build on, including aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder variants. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_020 because ViT-L is a bigger image backbone, roughly 1.3–1.6x or about 9–12 GPU hours. That is justified because the image encoder is likely a high-impact factor.

1. Evidence: swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L, with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, avgpool, concat), raised validation accuracy from 0.632 to 0.715. F1 rose with it (0.607 to 0.687). The ViT-L run was also cheaper (4.49 vs 7.27 GPU h), likely because its features are precomputed. The image encoder looks settled for now. Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) is the main open design choice still untested. 2. This experiment keeps the current best setup and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation, so any change in accuracy can be attributed to aggregation alone. 3. Attention-based multiprofile aggregation is a likely source of further gains, so this extends the strongest direction while answering an important open question. Its result will guide later tests of RNA encoders (PCA, scGPT) and fusion type. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_003 because of the transformer aggregator, roughly 5-7 GPU h, likely still below the ResNet50 run.

1) Evidence so far: the image encoder is the dominant factor. With the same scVI RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, ViT-L scored 0.715 accuracy versus 0.632 for ResNet50, and it was also cheaper (4.49 vs 7.27 GPU hours). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool only marginally (0.721 vs 0.715 accuracy), and its F1 was slightly lower, so aggregation looks like a minor factor. The RNA encoder and the fusion type have not been varied at all. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps scVI for scGPT. It isolates the effect of the RNA encoder, which is the largest remaining uncertainty and could plausibly give a bigger gain than fusion or aggregation changes. 3) It extends the best configuration while exploring a new dimension, and the result will guide the remaining 5 experiments (a weighted-fusion variant, or a PCA comparison if scGPT underperforms). Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5.5 GPU hours, similar to the earlier ViT-L runs with perhaps slightly more overhead from scGPT embeddings.

Evidence: ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.715-0.721 vs 0.632). Transformer and avgpool aggregation are about tied (0.721 vs 0.715, with F1 slightly favoring avgpool). The RNA encoder has a large effect: swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507. The pca_n2000 RNA encoder, an important design choice, is still completely untested. Test: this keeps the best configuration (config_002: ViT-L, transformer, concat) fixed and swaps scVI for PCA-2000. It isolates whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation beats scVI. Why now: since the RNA encoder has shown the largest swing so far, resolving this choice is worth more than testing the smaller fusion question (weighted vs concat) first. That can follow on whichever encoder wins. Expected cost: moderate, roughly 4-5 GPU hours, similar to config_002. PCA features are cheap to compute and the ViT-L multiprofile pipeline has been relatively inexpensive.

1. Evidence: Five experiments show scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.72 vs 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.715 vs 0.632) and was also cheaper. Transformer and avgpool aggregation are nearly tied (0.721 vs 0.715), so aggregation matters little. The remaining uncertainty is fusion: every run so far used concat, and weighted fusion is untested. 2. Test: config_026 keeps the best setup (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer) and changes only concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of fusion on top of the current best of 0.7207. 3. Why now: This is the most direct test that could beat the current best, and it settles the last major design choice in one controlled run. With 4 experiments left, the result tells us whether to pair weighted fusion with avgpool next (config_044), or to keep concat and check whether image-only or single-profile variants do better. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_002. That is cheaper than any resnet50 multiprofile run.

1) Evidence: the scvi_n200 RNA encoder with the imagenet_vit_l image encoder is clearly the strongest pairing (0.715 to 0.725). Swapping either encoder hurts a lot: scgpt gave 0.507, pca_n2000 gave 0.599 and resnet50 gave 0.632. Within this pairing, aggregation and fusion change accuracy only slightly. Transformer beat avgpool by about 0.006 under concat, and weighted beat concat by about 0.004 under transformer. These gaps are too small to read much into, and F1 is mixed (avgpool+concat has the highest F1 at 0.687). 2) Test: config_044 (scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the one untested cell in the aggregation × fusion grid for the best encoders. It shows whether weighted fusion helps independently of aggregation and whether avgpool+weighted can beat the current best of 0.725. 3) Why now: it exploits the best-supported region at low expected cost, about 3.5 to 4.5 GPU hours, similar to or cheaper than the transformer variants since avgpool is lighter. Riskier moves such as image-only or singleprofile runs can wait for the remaining 3 experiments.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_026 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion give only small, uncertain gains over avgpool and concat. The RNA encoder matters much more: replacing scVI with PCA dropped accuracy to 0.60, and scGPT dropped it to 0.51. ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50. 2) Open question: We have not tested whether the RNA branch adds anything beyond the image signal. Weak RNA encoders hurting the model this much suggests it might be dragging performance down. Image-only ViT-L with transformer aggregation (config_013) isolates the image contribution. It tests whether dropping RNA could match or beat 0.725, and it shows how much scVI really contributes. 3) Why this is the best use of the budget: All close neighbours of the current best are either already tested or use the clearly worse ResNet50 or RNA encoders. The modality question is the largest remaining uncertainty that could still produce a new best. Cost: without the RNA branch this should be cheaper than the multimodal ViT-L runs, roughly 3 to 4 GPU hours. That leaves 2 experiments to exploit whatever we learn.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder, beating pca_n2000 (0.60) and scgpt (0.51). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 by about 0.08. Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion give small, consistent gains, and the best result so far is config_026 at 0.725 accuracy. Image-only performance is very weak (0.26), so most of the predictive signal probably comes from RNA. The size of the image contribution in the fused model has never been isolated. 2) This experiment tests RNA-only scvi_n200 with transformer aggregation. It measures how much the image branch actually adds. If the image features mostly add noise, an RNA-only model could match or exceed 0.725. If it falls well short, that confirms fusion is essential and the last experiment should refine the multimodal scvi/vit_l design. 3) The remaining scvi multimodal options look weaker: the resnet50 variants should be worse given the 0.63 result, and single-profile variants lose aggregation. This configuration is a credible contender for the top score and also resolves the main open question about the modalities. Expected cost is low, about 1–2 GPU hours, much cheaper than the roughly 4-hour multimodal vit_l runs, since it has no large image encoder.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_026 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. The other choices are fairly well settled. scvi_n200 clearly beat pca_n2000 (0.599) and scgpt (0.507). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.715 vs 0.632 under matched avgpool/concat settings). Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion each gave only small gains of about 0.5 to 2 points. The one major axis never tested is the profile setting: every run used multiprofile. 2) This run tests whether a singleprofile model with the best-known components (scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted fusion) can match or beat the multiprofile best. Multiprofile aggregation could be adding noise rather than signal, and this is the largest remaining uncertainty. 3) Why this is the best final run: the remaining multiprofile variants mostly swap in components that were already clearly worse (ResNet50, PCA, scGPT), so they have little chance of beating 0.725. This configuration is the most plausible route to a new best, though it may well fall short of 0.725. Expected cost is low, likely about 2 to 3 GPU hours, below the roughly 3.6 to 4.8 hours of the multiprofile ViT runs because no multiprofile aggregation is needed.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so I can only rely on priors. In multimodal cellular profiling, combining RNA with imaging and aggregating over multiple profiles usually gives the highest accuracy. 2. What this tests: config_007 combines the strongest-looking option on each axis: multimodal, multiprofile with transformer aggregation, scVI-200 RNA embeddings (compact and well regularized) and the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, joined by weighted fusion. It sets a likely-high anchor that later runs can be compared against. Each later run can then change one factor (fusion, aggregation, encoders, or dropping a modality) to measure that factor's effect. 3. Why now: only the best accuracy within the budget counts, so starting near the likely optimum secures a strong result early. The remaining 9 runs can then refine it and test cheaper alternatives. Expected cost: high relative to the other options, because multiprofile transformer aggregation and the large ViT-L image representations are the most expensive pieces. The compact 200-dimensional scVI input keeps the RNA side cheap, and I accept the higher cost here because this design is the most likely top performer.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result so far. config_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1 at 3.6 GPU hours. With only one data point, we cannot tell which design choices drive that performance. The most important and most expensive open question is whether multiprofile aggregation is worth its cost. 2. What this tests: config_014 keeps the same encoders and fusion but uses a single profile with no aggregation.
