Expected cost is relatively low, about 3–4 GPU hours, similar to or slightly below config_025, since vit_l runs were the cheaper multimodal ones and avgpool avoids transformer overhead.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run yet, so every design axis is uncertain: modality, single vs. multiprofile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. Prior knowledge from cellular profiling suggests that multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation usually beat unimodal, single-profile models, but this has not been checked on this task. 2) What it tests: config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) is a strong but simple anchor. It combines both modalities and multiple profiles while using the most basic aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat) and compact encoders. It sets a baseline for the design family most likely to win. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, ViT-L, scGPT/PCA) or run a unimodal or single-profile ablation. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: it should give near-top accuracy early with a clean reference point for one-factor comparisons. Expected cost is moderate. Multiprofile multimodal training costs more than single-profile or unimodal runs, but the small scVI latent, ResNet50 and avgpool make it among the cheapest multiprofile multimodal options. It should cost well below transformer-aggregation or ViT-L variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1, so we have a reasonable baseline but no comparisons yet. The image encoder is a key untested choice, and a large pretrained ViT-L could plausibly give stronger morphological features than ResNet50. 2. What this tests: config_012 changes only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l and keeps every other setting the same. Any change in accuracy can therefore be attributed to the image backbone. 3. Why now: the image encoder probably has a larger effect than fusion or aggregation, and the answer will steer most later multimodal choices. With 8 experiments left, settling it early is worthwhile. Expected cost is moderately higher than the 7.27 GPU-hour baseline, perhaps about 1.3–1.8x, because ViT-L features are larger. That cost is justified because this is likely to point toward the best-performing configuration.

Evidence: with the RNA encoder (scvi_n200), multiprofile setting, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.632 to 0.715 (F1 0.607 to 0.687). It also cut training cost (4.49 vs 7.27 GPU h). So ViT-L is the image encoder to build on. Uncertainty: aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder are all still untested. Aggregation is likely the most influential of these in the multiprofile setting, because a transformer can learn attention over profiles while avgpool simply averages them. What this tests: config_024 keeps the best configuration (config_012) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. That gives a clean one-factor comparison on a design choice that could add substantial accuracy. Why now: it exploits the strong ViT-L signal while resolving a major open choice early, so later experiments (weighted fusion, scGPT or PCA RNA encoders) can build on the better aggregator. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_012 because of the transformer aggregator, roughly 5-7 GPU hours. That is likely still at or below the ResNet50 run's cost and justified by the potential gain.

1) Evidence: three experiments show the image encoder matters most. ImageNet ViT-L (0.715 to 0.721 accuracy) clearly beats ResNet50 (0.632), and it was also cheaper to train (about 4.5 vs 7.3 GPU hours). Transformer aggregation was only marginally better than avgpool on accuracy (0.721 vs 0.715) and slightly worse on F1, so aggregation looks like a minor factor. The RNA encoder (all runs used scVI) and the fusion method (all runs used concat) are completely unexplored. 2) This run keeps the best known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps scVI for the scGPT foundation-model embeddings. Changing only the RNA encoder isolates its effect, which is likely larger than the effect of fusion type. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because it reduces uncertainty on a potentially high-impact design choice while staying in the region that already performs best, so it can directly yield a new best result. The outcome will also guide later tests of PCA and weighted fusion. Expected cost is moderate, similar to the earlier ViT-L multiprofile runs at about 4.5 to 5.5 GPU hours; scGPT embeddings may add slight overhead but should cost well below the ResNet50 run.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_024 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy. config_012 differs only in avgpool aggregation and reached 0.715. Both clearly beat ResNet50 (0.632) and scGPT (0.507). Fusion type has never been tested, and every run so far used concat. 2) This experiment changes only the fusion step of the best configuration, from concat to weighted, so any accuracy or F1 change can be attributed to fusion alone. 3) It exploits the strongest region found so far while resolving an untested, important design choice, and the result will guide the remaining runs (for example, a later pca_n2000 comparison). Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_024, since weighted fusion adds little compute over concat.

1. Evidence: The image encoder and RNA encoder have the largest effects so far. imagenet_vit_l clearly beats resnet50 (0.715 vs 0.632 with avgpool/concat). scvi_n200 clearly beats scgpt (0.721 vs 0.507 with the same ViT/transformer/concat setup). Aggregation and fusion change results only slightly: transformer is about 0.006 above avgpool, and weighted is about 0.004 above concat. These gaps are small enough to be noise, though the best run (config_036, scvi + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725) also had the lowest cost. The main untested design choice is the third RNA encoder, pca_n2000. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best known setup and swaps only scvi_n200 for pca_n2000. This isolates whether a simple high-dimensional PCA representation beats the learned scVI embedding. 3. Why now: Trying the remaining minor aggregation/fusion variants offers little expected gain, while an RNA encoder that beats scVI is the most plausible route to a clearly higher accuracy. Answering it now leaves 3 experiments to exploit the result. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3.6–5 GPU hours, similar to the other ViT-L multiprofile runs. The 2000-dimensional RNA input may add a little overhead, but it should cost much less than the 7.3-hour ResNet50 run.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 plus imagenet_vit_l is clearly the strongest combination so far (0.715 to 0.725). Changing aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) or fusion (concat vs weighted) moved accuracy by only about 0.01, which is within noise. Every experiment so far has been multiprofile, so the profile setting has not been tested at all. 2) This run keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion from config_036 but switches to singleprofile. It tests whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed, or whether a single profile matches or beats it. 3) This is a better use of the budget than another small aggregation or fusion tweak, such as config_026, which is unlikely to give a meaningful gain. It removes uncertainty on a major untested design choice that could shift accuracy substantially in either direction, and it guides the last two experiments. Expected cost is low: singleprofile skips multiprofile aggregation, so I expect it to be cheaper than the roughly 3.6 to 4.7 GPU hours of the vit_l multiprofile runs.

1. Evidence: the strongest region is clearly scVI RNA + ImageNet ViT-L + multiprofile. Within it, avgpool/concat scored 0.715, transformer/concat 0.721 and transformer/weighted 0.725 (best so far). Swapping in other components hurt badly: scGPT 0.507, PCA 0.586, ResNet50 0.632, single-profile 0.537. The gaps between aggregation and fusion choices are small, about 0.005 to 0.01 and within likely noise. The avgpool/weighted cell is the only untested combination in this 2x2 grid. 2. Test: config_026 completes the grid. It shows whether weighted fusion's small gain holds with simpler avgpool aggregation, and whether avgpool/weighted can match or beat the current best. 3. Why now: this is the most direct exploitation of the best region. Its odds of a new top score are better than options already shown to be weak, such as scGPT, PCA, ResNet50 or single-profile. An image-only test would be more uncertain, since the large drops with weaker RNA encoders suggest a good RNA encoder adds value. Expected cost is moderate, about 3.5 to 4.5 GPU hours, similar to or slightly below the transformer variants. That leaves one experiment for a final exploit or a check on modality.

1) Evidence: the scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l multiprofile grid is now fully tested across both aggregations and both fusions. All four sit in a narrow 0.706–0.725 band, with the best being config_036 (transformer, weighted, 0.725). The RNA encoder matters a great deal: swapping in scgpt (0.507) or pca_n2000 (0.586) caused large drops. ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.716 vs 0.632 in matched configs), and multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin. 2) Open question: does the RNA branch actually help, or does the ViT-L image signal drive most of the accuracy? This experiment runs image-only ViT-L with multiprofile transformer aggregation, keeping the best-performing image and aggregation settings. If it matches or beats 0.725, that would show RNA fusion adds little and the cheaper unimodal model is preferable. If it falls clearly short, that confirms config_036 as the best design. 3) Why this is the best use of the experiment: the remaining multimodal variants either use ResNet50, scgpt or pca_n2000, which have all lost consistently, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This is the last untested design choice with a realistic chance of matching or exceeding the current best. Expected cost is low to moderate, likely below the roughly 3.6–4.8 GPU hours of the multimodal ViT-L multiprofile runs, because there is no RNA encoder or fusion step.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI-n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion) at 0.725. The concat and avgpool variants reached 0.706–0.721, and all four scVI + ViT-L multiprofile combinations are now tested. scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (scGPT 0.51, PCA 0.59). ResNet50 trailed ViT-L by about 8 points (0.63 vs 0.715). Image-only reached just 0.26, so most of the signal appears to come from RNA. 2. Question: Does the image branch actually add value, or does scVI RNA-only with transformer aggregation (config_004) match or beat the multimodal best? 3. Why this experiment: None of the remaining multimodal options looks likely to beat 0.725, since they all use weaker encoders such as ResNet50, PCA or scGPT. Swapping in ResNet50 (config_003) is expected to lose accuracy. Dropping the weak image modality is the most plausible untested route to a higher score. It also settles an important design question about whether the image modality is needed. Expected cost is low, likely around 1–2 GPU hours versus about 3.6–4.8 for the ViT-L multimodal runs, because it skips image processing.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we have no data on any design choice. Prior knowledge suggests that combining RNA and image data, aggregating over multiple profiles and using a learned transformer aggregator are the most likely to give high accuracy. 2) This run sets a strong anchor using the expected-best structure (multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). It pairs that structure with mid-sized encoders: compact scVI (200 dimensions) for RNA and ResNet50 for images. Later runs can then change one factor at a time against this baseline, such as the encoder (scGPT, ViT-L), the aggregation (avgpool) or the fusion (concat), or try single-modality and single-profile ablations. 3) It is the best first use of the budget because it is likely to score well on its own while avoiding the heaviest encoders. Expected relative cost is moderate to high: multiprofile transformer aggregation with multimodal processing is costly, but it is cheaper than the scGPT or ViT-L variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1 for 6.22 GPU hours. With one data point, no design choice is resolved, and the RNA encoder is a major untested factor. 2) Test: config_042 changes only the RNA encoder from scVI to the scGPT foundation model and keeps everything else as in config_001. The comparison is therefore clean and shows whether richer pretrained RNA embeddings improve accuracy, using F1 as a cross-check. 3) Why now: in multimodal cellular profiling the RNA branch often carries much of the signal, so the RNA encoder is a likely lever for the best final accuracy. A one-factor change also keeps the result interpretable for later steps, such as trying ViT-L image features or avgpool aggregation. It is better value than switching to ViT-L first because it avoids the extra cost of a large image backbone while still testing a high-impact choice. Expected cost: similar to or slightly above config_001 (roughly 6–8 GPU hours), depending on how scGPT embeddings are produced.

1) Evidence: Holding resnet50, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion fixed, scvi_n200 (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1) clearly beat scgpt (0.494 acc, 0.453 F1). scgpt also took about twice the GPU hours. So scvi_n200 is the strongest RNA encoder found so far. The image encoder has not been varied yet, and it is a major untested design choice. 2) This experiment keeps the best-known setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) and swaps resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This is justified because the image encoder could plausibly yield the best accuracy.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder has had the largest effect so far. With resnet50, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion held fixed, scvi_n200 reached 0.713 accuracy and scgpt reached 0.494, and scgpt cost about twice the GPU hours. Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l in the scvi setup gave a small gain (0.725 vs 0.713) at lower cost (3.6 vs 6.2 h), though F1 was slightly lower (0.685 vs 0.695), so that edge is modest. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is still untested. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup (vit_l, transformer, weighted) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. Expected cost is low to moderate, roughly similar to config_015 at about 3.5–5 GPU hours. pca features are cheap to compute, but the 2000-dimensional input may add slightly more cost than scvi's 200 dimensions.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder matters most so far. scvi_n200 (0.713 and 0.725) clearly beats pca_n2000 (0.586) and scgpt (0.494). imagenet_vit_l slightly beat resnet50 when paired with scvi_n200 (0.725 vs 0.713), and it trained faster (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h). However, all four experiments used transformer aggregation with weighted fusion, so the aggregation and fusion choices are still untested. 2. Test: This run keeps the best known setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion) and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. That isolates whether transformer aggregation is actually needed or whether simpler pooling does as well or better. 3. Why now: Aggregation is a major design axis with no evidence yet, and changing only this one variable from the current best gives a clean comparison. That keeps total GPU hours down while leaving budget to test fusion (e.g., config_044) and single-modality baselines afterwards.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.71–0.72 accuracy, versus 0.49 for scGPT and 0.59 for PCA). Transformer aggregation slightly beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706, with F1 0.685 vs 0.667). ViT-L matches or beats ResNet50 on accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713) and costs less (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h). Fusion is the one major design choice not yet tested: every completed run used weighted fusion. 2. What this tests: config_044 keeps the current best setup (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer) and switches only the fusion to concat. This isolates the fusion effect and is the most direct way to improve on config_015. 3. Why it is the best next use: it either finds a new best or confirms weighted fusion, which then focuses the last 3 experiments elsewhere. Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. With scVI, accuracy is 0.71-0.725; with PCA it is 0.586 and with scGPT 0.494. Image encoder, aggregation and fusion changes moved accuracy by only about 0.01-0.02. Transformer aggregation slightly beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706), and weighted fusion slightly beat concat (0.725 vs 0.721). These differences are small and may not be meaningful. The biggest untested question is whether the image modality helps at all, since performance tracks RNA quality so closely. This experiment tests an RNA-only scVI model with multiprofile transformer aggregation. It isolates the image contribution while keeping the best RNA and aggregation choices. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.725, the remaining budget shifts toward cheaper RNA-centric variants. If it falls clearly below, that confirms multimodal fusion and points the last runs at refining the scVI + ViT-L multimodal setup. Evidence: the scvi_n200 RNA encoder is clearly the best choice. Its runs score 0.70-0.725, against 0.586 for pca_n2000 and 0.494 for scgpt. The best run is config_015 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy, 3.6 GPU hours). Its tested neighbours all score slightly lower: resnet50 0.713, avgpool 0.706 and concat 0.721. So fusion, aggregation and image encoder now look like small, nearly settled effects. The largest remaining unknown is the profile setting, because every multimodal run so far has been multiprofile. Test: config_035 keeps the best RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion and switches to singleprofile. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps. Why now: other untested neighbours of config_015, such as config_009 and config_032, are predicted to land near or below 0.725 and would add little information. This run probes the one unexplored axis and could find a better or cheaper optimum. With 2 experiments left, the last runs can then exploit whichever profile setting wins. Expected cost is low, likely below config_015's 3.6 GPU hours, because it has no multiprofile aggregation.

1) Evidence: The strongest pattern is scVI RNA encoding with multiprofile transformer aggregation. All three such runs scored 0.713 to 0.725, while scGPT (0.494) and PCA (0.586) RNA encoders were far worse. Single-profile (0.537), avgpool (0.706) and RNA-only (0.653) were also clearly weaker. Within the top group, the differences are small and inside run-to-run noise. ViT-L with weighted fusion has the best accuracy (0.725, config_015). ResNet50 with weighted fusion has the best F1 (0.695 vs 0.685, config_001). Concat fusion matched weighted fusion closely on ViT-L (0.721). 2) Test: config_009 is the only untested configuration in this top group (scVI, ResNet50, transformer, concat). It checks whether ResNet50's F1 advantage combined with concat fusion can push accuracy above 0.725. 3) Why this experiment: With two experiments left, exploiting the best-supported region gives the highest chance of improving the best accuracy. The alternatives have weaker prospects. Image-only runs are unlikely to beat multimodal, since adding images to RNA added about 0.07. Avgpool and other encoders already underperform. Expected cost is relatively high, similar to config_001's 6.2 GPU hours, because ResNet50 multiprofile transformer runs have been the slowest scVI runs. The higher accuracy potential justifies this cost over cheaper but weaker options.

1. Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder is clearly the decisive factor. scVI multimodal runs scored 0.69-0.725, while scGPT (0.494) and PCA (0.586) were much worse, and RNA-only scVI reached 0.653. With scVI, ViT-L slightly beat ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.713 weighted; 0.721 vs 0.688 concat). Weighted and concat fusion were nearly tied for ViT-L. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706 with weighted fusion). Single-profile runs were much worse. The best so far is config_015 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725). 2. Test: the strong transformer combinations are already covered, so the only untested multiprofile scVI + ViT-L variant is avgpool with concat fusion. This checks whether concat fusion offsets the avgpool penalty, since fusion and aggregation might interact. 3. Why this one: it stays in the best-performing region (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile). That makes it the most plausible remaining chance to beat 0.725. Image-only, PCA and scGPT options have little prospect of winning, and the ResNet50 avgpool variants are expected to be lower. Expected relative cost is moderate, about 4.5-5 GPU hours, similar to config_003 and config_044.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so I am relying only on priors. In multimodal cellular profiling, combining RNA and image data and aggregating over multiple profiles usually beats unimodal or single-profile setups. 2) Test: config_022 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) sets a strong anchor for what I expect is the best-performing family. It uses a compact scVI embedding, a mid-size image backbone and the simplest fusion method. 3) Why now: it lands in the likely-optimal region without the extra cost of a ViT-L image encoder or scGPT, which keeps cost moderate. 1) Evidence: There is only one result so far. The full multimodal, multiprofile setup (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. One point gives no evidence about which design choice drives performance. 2) Test: This keeps every setting the same except the image encoder, which changes from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Because only one factor changes, the result directly shows whether a stronger image representation helps. The image backbone is likely one of the biggest levers for multimodal accuracy. 3) Why now: If ViT-L helps, later experiments can build on it by trying other RNA encoders, weighted fusion and avgpool aggregation. If it does not help, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 for the rest of the budget. Settling this high-impact choice early is worth more than smaller tweaks like fusion type. Why now: The RNA encoder is likely to move accuracy more than the fusion or aggregation choice, so settling it early lets the remaining 7 runs focus on the best encoder pair. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + concat, accuracy 0.721, F1 0.681). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L gained about 3 points. Swapping scVI for scGPT lost about 21 points. Evidence: the RNA encoder matters most so far. scvi_n200 clearly beats pca_n2000 (0.599) and scgpt (0.507) when paired with ViT-L. ViT-L beats ResNet50 when paired with scVI (0.721 vs 0.688). 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.72 vs 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_013 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_013 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Several choices now look fairly settled. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer edges out avgpool, and weighted fusion slightly beats concat. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_013 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The other design axes look settled. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer aggregation beats avgpool, and multiprofile beats single-profile. Image-only scores only 0.26, so almost all predictive signal seems to come from RNA. Weighted fusion edges out concat (0.725 vs 0.721), which hints that down-weighting the image branch helps. The image branch could be adding mostly noise. 2. Test: config_031 is the scVI RNA-only multiprofile transformer model. It tests whether dropping the weak image modality matches or beats the current best, which is the main untested design choice. 3. Why now: The remaining multimodal variants (ResNet50, avgpool, other RNA encoders) changed only factors that already underperformed, so they are unlikely to exceed 0.725. This is the main remaining candidate with a realistic chance of a higher score. If it does not win, it still confirms config_013 as the best and leaves the final experiment for a targeted check. Expected cost: lower than the multimodal runs (about 1.5–3 GPU hours versus 3.6–5 GPU hours), since there is no image encoder or fusion.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_013 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, accuracy 0.725). scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder: PCA reached 0.599 and scGPT 0.507. ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688 under concat fusion). Transformer aggregation slightly beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706 under weighted fusion), and weighted fusion only slightly beat concat (0.725 vs 0.721). 2. Test: among the untested configurations, the near-optimal variants that keep scVI are config_018 (ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and config_030 (ResNet50, transformer, weighted). Additive estimates from the history give config_018 about 0.70 and config_030 about 0.69, because the image-encoder gap is larger than the aggregation gap. This run tests whether concat fusion with avgpool closes the aggregation gap, completing the fusion-by-aggregation grid for the best encoder pair. 3. Why this run: it is the remaining configuration most likely to match or exceed 0.725, though no option is strongly expected to beat config_013. Cheaper unimodal or single-profile options are far below the leader and cannot help the final best accuracy. Expected cost is similar to the other multiprofile ViT-L runs, roughly 4.5 to 5 GPU hours.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation or fusion works best. The usual prior in cellular profiling is that combining RNA with images and aggregating over multiple profiles gives the highest accuracy. That prior is unconfirmed here. 2. What this tests: config_009 combines RNA and images over multiple profiles, so it directly checks whether that design is as strong as expected. Its components are relatively light: the compact scVI-200 RNA encoder, the ResNet50 image encoder, simple average pooling and weighted fusion. This makes it a cheap reference point for later single-variable comparisons, such as switching to a transformer aggregator, a ViT-L image encoder, scGPT or concat fusion. 3. Why now: Testing the likely-best region early, at moderate cost, gives a strong baseline to improve on in the remaining 9 experiments. It avoids spending heavily on the largest combinations before the main direction is confirmed. Expected cost: moderate. It costs more than single-profile or single-modality runs, but clearly less than multimodal multiprofile setups using ViT-L, scGPT or a transformer aggregator.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: Only one result exists. The multimodal, multiprofile setup (scVI-200 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. This is a reasonable baseline, but we have no evidence yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_010 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. That isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. Aggregation is the main extra design choice that multiprofile models introduce, so the answer guides many remaining configurations. 3. Why this is the best next use: a single-variable comparison gives a clean result, and the baseline is already strong, so this stays close to a promising region. I expect it to cost moderately more than the baseline, roughly 1.2-1.5x its 5.9 GPU hours, because of the transformer aggregator. That is cheaper than switching to the ViT-L image encoder, which I plan to test next depending on this result.

1. Evidence: The two runs differ only in aggregation, and the transformer beat avgpool (acc 0.713 vs 0.678, F1 0.695 vs 0.646). That is a consistent gain, though it rests on a single comparison. Image encoder, RNA encoder and fusion are still untested. 2. What this tests: config_043 keeps the best setup so far (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer, weighted) and swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This gives a clean one-variable test of whether a stronger pretrained image representation adds accuracy on top of transformer aggregation. 3. Why now: The image encoder is likely one of the highest-impact remaining choices, and building on the current best config keeps the comparison interpretable. With 7 experiments left, the result can redirect later tests of the RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA) and fusion (concat). Expected cost: higher than config_010, roughly 1.3–1.6x (about 8–10 GPU hours), because of the larger ViT-L features. This is justified because the configuration is a plausible candidate for the best accuracy.

Evidence: Among multiprofile, multimodal, weighted-fusion runs, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 3.5 points of accuracy (0.713 vs 0.678 with resnet50). Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l under transformer gave a further small accuracy gain (0.725). That ViT run was also cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU hours). The RNA encoder is the largest untested design choice: only scvi_n200 has been tried, and scgpt and pca_n2000 remain open. Test: config_005 keeps everything from the current best (config_043: multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps scvi_n200 for scgpt. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding improves the multimodal model. Why now: with 6 experiments left, settling the RNA encoder axis on top of the strongest backbone is the most informative single-factor change. It may also directly give a new best. Fusion type (concat) can be tested afterwards on whichever RNA encoder wins. Expected cost: similar to config_043, roughly 3.5 to 5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more if scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy). The transformer clearly beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678 with ResNet50). ViT-L slightly beat ResNet50 on accuracy and was cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h). The RNA encoder was the largest effect seen: swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.52. The third RNA option, PCA (pca_n2000), has not been tested at all. 2) This run keeps the best setup and swaps only scVI for PCA. That isolates whether a simple, high-dimensional PCA representation of the RNA data matches or beats scVI. 3) The RNA encoder is the highest-variance factor so far, and one option is still unknown, so this is the most informative test. It could also directly set a new best. Fusion (concat vs weighted) is also untested but has likely smaller effect, and can be tested next using whichever RNA encoder wins. Expected cost is similar to config_043, about 3.5–4 GPU h. That is moderate, since the 2000-dimensional PCA input is slightly larger, and cheaper than the ResNet50 runs.

1. Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. With ViT-L, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion, scVI reached 0.725, versus 0.586 for PCA and 0.520 for scGPT. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 3.5 points with ResNet50 (0.713 vs 0.678). ViT-L slightly beat ResNet50 on accuracy and was cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h). Fusion type is the one important axis not yet tested, since every run so far used weighted fusion. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_043) fixed and changes only the fusion to concat. That isolates the effect of the fusion strategy at the current optimum. 3. It exploits the strongest direction while answering the largest remaining uncertainty, and the result will guide the last three experiments. Retrying avgpool or the weaker RNA encoders is less likely to help, given the evidence above. Expected cost is low, roughly 3.5–4 GPU hours, similar to config_043 and cheaper than the ResNet50 runs.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725. Concat fusion (0.721) is essentially tied. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 3.5 points. The RNA encoder matters most: swapping scVI for scGPT or PCA dropped accuracy by 14-20 points. The image encoder matters little: ResNet50 to ViT-L gained only about 1 point. Modality has not been tested at all, so it is still unclear whether the image branch helps. 2) This experiment tests RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation over multiple profiles. It shows whether the scVI RNA signal drives performance on its own, and whether the image branch adds information or noise. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.725, we find a stronger or cheaper optimum. If it falls clearly below, multimodal is confirmed and the remaining budget goes to profile-setting or fusion refinements around config_043. 3) It is the best use of the next slot because modality is the largest untested design choice, and the evidence that RNA dominates makes this a credible contender rather than just a baseline. Expected cost is low: likely under 3 GPU hours, cheaper than any multimodal run, because there is no ViT-L image processing.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.725 with it versus 0.586 for pca_n2000 and 0.520 for scgpt). ViT-L edges out ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.713). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678). Weighted and concat fusion are nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721). The current best is config_043 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted, 0.725). 1) Evidence: the best runs share scvi_n200 RNA, multiprofile input and transformer aggregation. The top result is config_043 (ViT-L, weighted) at 0.725. ViT-L with concat (config_047) reached 0.721, so the fusion type barely matters with ViT-L. ResNet50 with weighted fusion (config_010) reached 0.713 and has the highest F1 so far (0.695), so ResNet50 remains competitive. Avgpool aggregation lost about 3.5 points versus transformer with ResNet50, and scGPT or PCA RNA encoders and single-profile input all performed much worse. The open question is whether the ResNet50 path can overtake the ViT-L leader. 2) Test: config_006 keeps the winning scvi + multiprofile + transformer recipe and adds concat fusion to the ResNet50 encoder. It is the only untested combination in that top family. 3) Why now: given its strong F1 and the small gap to the leader, it has a plausible chance of beating 0.725. Image-only or avgpool variants are less likely to win. Expected cost is relatively high, about 6 GPU hours, similar to config_010, because it combines multiprofile, multimodal processing and a transformer. I accept that cost because this is the most likely remaining candidate for the best accuracy.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is scVI + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion (config_043, 0.725). Concat fusion is about equal (0.721). The scVI RNA encoder clearly beats scGPT (0.520) and PCA (0.586). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (0.537). The one design choice not yet tested on the strongest backbone pair is aggregation. With ResNet50, avgpool scored about 3.5 points below transformer (0.678 vs 0.713), but ViT-L features are stronger and may need less learned aggregation, so that gap may shrink or reverse. 2) Test: config_011 holds everything from the best config fixed and swaps transformer for avgpool. This isolates aggregation on the best scVI/ViT-L/weighted combination. 3) Why this is the best final pick: it is the only untested neighbor of the top config with a realistic chance of beating 0.725. The alternatives are weaker bets: image-only and RNA-only models remove a modality, and scGPT or PCA variants have underperformed consistently. Expected cost is relatively low, roughly 3–3.5 GPU hours, similar to or slightly below config_043 because avgpool is cheaper than a transformer aggregator. A loss would not reduce the best result already found.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so every design axis is open. These axes are modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. My prior is that multimodal, multiprofile models are most likely to reach the highest accuracy, but that is still untested. 2. What this tests: config_037 is a mid-complexity anchor in that region: multimodal, multiprofile, the compact scVI-200 RNA encoder, a ResNet50 image encoder, average-pool aggregation and concat fusion. It gives a strong baseline. Later runs can then change one axis at a time: ViT-L instead of ResNet50, a transformer instead of average pooling, scGPT or PCA instead of scVI, weighted instead of concat fusion, and single-modality or single-profile ablations. 3. Why now: Starting in the likely high-accuracy region, with cheaper components, sets a competitive best-so-far early without paying for the largest models before the basic design is confirmed. Expected cost: moderate. Multiprofile and multimodal processing add cost, but the small scVI latent space, ResNet50 and average pooling keep it well below ViT-L, scGPT or transformer-aggregation variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one data point. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1, at 7.27 GPU hours. We do not yet know which design axis matters most. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. That gives a clean one-factor comparison of image representation quality, which I expect to be one of the largest drivers of accuracy for morphology-based profiling. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: if the ViT-L result is clearly better, later experiments can build on it by testing transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and other RNA encoders. If it is not better, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 and explore aggregation or RNA encoders instead. Either outcome sharpens the search early. Expected cost is moderately higher than the baseline, roughly 1.3–1.8x (about 9–13 GPU hours), because ViT-L is a larger image encoder. This is justified because the image encoder is a high-impact choice.

Evidence: the two completed runs differ only in image encoder. ImageNet ViT-L reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1, about 8 points above ResNet50, and it trained faster (4.49 vs 7.27 GPU hours). That makes the scVI + ViT-L + multiprofile + concat setup the strongest base so far. Uncertainty: the effects of aggregation, RNA encoder and fusion are still unknown. Aggregation may matter most, because multiprofile inputs could benefit from learned attention across profiles rather than simple averaging. This test: config_006 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, while keeping the best setup otherwise unchanged. The result will cleanly show whether attention-based aggregation improves on averaging. Why now: it exploits the clear ViT-L win while resolving one key design choice, and the answer will guide the remaining experiments (scGPT vs PCA RNA encoders, weighted vs concat fusion). Expected cost: moderately higher than config_004 because of the transformer aggregator, likely about 5-7 GPU hours. It should still be no more expensive than the ResNet50 run.

1) Evidence: switching the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l gave a large gain (0.632 to 0.715 accuracy) and was also cheaper (4.5 vs 7.3 GPU h). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool only slightly (0.721 vs 0.715 accuracy, with F1 slightly lower), which is within noise. The biggest open question is the RNA encoder: every run so far used scvi_n200. Fusion type is also untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best-so-far setup (vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. That isolates the effect of a pretrained foundation-model RNA encoder, which could plausibly shift accuracy by more than the aggregation or fusion choices would. 3) Settling the RNA encoder choice early lets the remaining 5 experiments exploit the best encoder, for example by then testing weighted fusion or pca_n2000. Expected cost is moderate, around 5 to 6 GPU h. That is similar to config_006, perhaps slightly higher if scGPT embeddings are larger, and still below the resnet50 run.

1) Evidence: scVI_n200 with ImageNet ViT-L is clearly the strongest pairing so far. It scored 0.715 and 0.721, well above ResNet50 (0.632) and far above scGPT (0.507). Transformer aggregation is only marginally better than avgpool (+0.006 accuracy, with slightly lower F1), so that choice is nearly tied. Fusion is the one major design axis not yet tested, since every run so far used concat. 2) This experiment keeps the best-performing setup (scVI + ViT-L + transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of the fusion strategy. 3) Weighted fusion could plausibly improve on concat by balancing the two modalities, so this is both a direct attempt at a new best and a way to settle an untested design choice. Either outcome guides the remaining 5 experiments, for example whether to try weighted fusion with avgpool or with PCA RNA features. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_006. That is cheaper than the ResNet50 run and well within budget.

Evidence: the RNA encoder is the design choice with the largest effect so far. With imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation and concat fusion, scvi_n200 reached 0.721 accuracy and scgpt only 0.507. ViT-L is clearly better than ResNet50 (0.715 vs 0.632 under avgpool and concat). Aggregation and fusion changes moved accuracy by only about 0.005–0.01, with config_043 (scvi, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) best at 0.725. pca_n2000 is still completely untested, so it is the main remaining uncertainty that could produce a sizeable gain. This experiment swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 in the current best setup. That shows directly whether PCA features beat scVI, and with 4 experiments left the answer tells us which RNA encoder to refine further. Other options look less useful. Avgpool or single-profile versions of the best setup are expected to give small or negative changes. Image-only or RNA-only runs would mainly serve as ablations rather than raise the best score. Expected cost is similar to config_043, about 3.6–4.7 GPU hours (multiprofile with transformer and ViT-L), though the 2000-dimensional PCA input may add a little.

1) Evidence: scVI_n200 with ViT-L is clearly the strongest encoder pair (0.715-0.725). The alternatives, scGPT (0.507), PCA (0.586) and ResNet50 (0.632), are much worse. Among scVI+ViT-L runs, the aggregation and fusion choices change accuracy by only about 0.01. The best so far is config_043 (transformer, weighted) at 0.725. A key axis is still completely untested: every run has been multiprofile. 2) This experiment keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile, with no aggregation. It directly tests whether multiprofile aggregation is actually helping. 3) The remaining scVI+ViT-L multiprofile variant (config_048, avgpool+weighted) would likely land around 0.72 and is unlikely to beat 0.725. The profile-setting question has a larger potential payoff and resolves a major uncertainty while 3 experiments remain. If singleprofile is competitive or better, later runs can exploit it. If it is worse, multiprofile is confirmed and we can return to refining config_043's neighborhood. Expected cost is relatively low, probably below the ~3.6-4.7 GPU hours of multiprofile ViT-L runs, because no multiprofile aggregation is needed.

1) Evidence: every strong result uses multiprofile with scVI RNA and ViT-L images (0.715 to 0.725). The best is config_043 (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725. The RNA encoder matters a lot: scGPT gave 0.507 and PCA gave 0.586. ResNet50 and single-profile runs were clearly worse. Within the scVI/ViT-L multiprofile group, transformer beat avgpool by only about 0.006, and weighted beat concat by only about 0.004. Both gaps are small and could be noise. The only untested combination in this group is avgpool with weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_048 checks whether weighted fusion still helps, or helps more, with the simpler avgpool aggregation. It also shows whether the transformer advantage is real or noise. It also has the best avgpool F1 so far (0.687, higher than the transformer runs), so it has a realistic chance of beating 0.725. 3) Why now: it exploits the most promising area at moderate cost. Expected cost is about 3.5 to 4.5 GPU hours, similar to or slightly below the transformer runs, since avgpool is cheaper than transformer aggregation. Exploring the weak areas (scGPT, PCA, ResNet50, single-profile) is unlikely to produce a new best with only 2 experiments left.

1) Evidence: the scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l multiprofile family is now fully mapped across aggregation (avgpool/transformer) and fusion (concat/weighted). All four sit at 0.706-0.725 accuracy, with the best being config_043 at 0.725 (transformer, weighted). Image encoder choice matters most: resnet50 drops accuracy to 0.63, while vit_l is consistently strong. RNA encoder choice is volatile: scgpt (0.51) and pca_n2000 (0.59) sharply hurt performance, so a weak RNA stream can degrade the fused model. The other untested multimodal options use resnet50, pca or scgpt, which the evidence says are inferior, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. 2) This experiment tests the main unresolved design question: does the vit_l image stream alone, with transformer aggregation over profiles, match or exceed multimodal fusion? If RNA adds noise or redundancy, image-only could set a new best. Either way, it shows how much the scvi stream contributes. 3) It is the highest-upside remaining option under a 2-experiment budget. Expected cost is lower than the multimodal runs (about 3-4 GPU hours vs 3.6-4.8), since no RNA encoder or fusion is needed. That leaves the final experiment to exploit whichever direction wins.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, beating PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.507). ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 8 points (0.715 vs 0.631 under avgpool/concat). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (0.537). Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion give only small gains of about 0.005-0.01. Image-only ViT-L is very weak (0.26), so RNA carries most of the signal. Every untested multimodal neighbour of the best config swaps in a component already shown to be worse. config_050 swaps in ResNet50, which would likely land near 0.64. config_051 and the other singleprofile options would likely land near 0.54. 2) This experiment tests the one major untested design choice near the optimum: does the image branch add real signal, or does it partly add noise that weighted fusion only partly suppresses? scVI RNA-only with transformer multiprofile aggregation answers this directly. 3) This is the final experiment, so only a chance to beat 0.725 matters. The swap-in neighbours have low expected upside. RNA-only scVI is the only remaining option with a plausible, if modest, chance of matching or exceeding the multimodal best, since ResNet's large deficit hints that weaker image features can hurt. It also cleanly settles whether the multimodal gain is real. Expected cost is low: with no image branch, likely about 1-2 GPU hours, well below the 3.6-4.8 hours of multimodal multiprofile runs.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. Prior knowledge from multimodal cellular profiling suggests three things: combining RNA and imaging usually beats either modality alone, aggregating multiple profiles beats single-profile inputs, and a learned transformer aggregator often beats average pooling. 2) What this tests: config_014 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA encoder, resnet50 image encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is a strong but moderately priced anchor that likely sits near the top of the space. It sets a high baseline for later one-factor comparisons: swapping the RNA encoder (scgpt or pca), the image encoder (ViT-L), the aggregation (avgpool) or the fusion (weighted), or dropping to single-modality or single-profile runs. 3) Why now: because only the best accuracy counts, an early high-probability candidate secures a good result and makes later comparisons informative. It also keeps cost down by avoiding the heavier ViT-L and scGPT backbones. Expected relative cost is medium-high: multiprofile transformer aggregation with multimodal processing costs more than single-modality or single-profile runs, but less than ViT-L or scGPT multimodal variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_014 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1 for 5.16 GPU hours. One point cannot tell us which component drives performance, and the image encoder is one of the biggest untested architectural choices. 2) Test: config_002 keeps every other setting identical and swaps ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. Because only one factor changes, the result directly shows whether a stronger image backbone improves accuracy within this strong-seeming multimodal and multiprofile setup. 3) Why now: the image encoder decision affects about half the remaining search space. Settling it early lets later experiments vary the RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion on the better backbone. It also has a real chance of producing the new best result. Expected cost is somewhat higher than config_014, roughly 1.3–1.8x (about 7–9 GPU hours), because ViT-L gives larger representations. That cost is justified given how much this choice affects the rest of the search.

1. Evidence: Swapping the image encoder from ResNet50 (config_014, 0.688 acc) to ImageNet ViT-L (config_002, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1) improved both accuracy and F1, with everything else fixed (scVI, multiprofile, transformer, concat). ViT-L was also slightly cheaper (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU h). The RNA encoder is now the largest untested design choice. 2. Test: config_004 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT, a pretrained foundation model that may give richer transcriptomic features. Evidence: the best result so far is scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat at 0.721 accuracy. That ViT-L setup beat ResNet50 (0.688) with otherwise identical settings. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT dropped accuracy sharply to 0.507, so the RNA encoder appears to be the highest-impact choice tested so far. The third RNA option, pca_n2000, is still untested and could match or beat scVI. Test: config_046 keeps the best setup fixed (ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This isolates whether PCA features beat scVI. Fusion (config_049) and avgpool aggregation (config_025) can follow on the winning encoder. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + concat, 0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). The RNA encoder now looks well resolved. With ViT-L, scVI (0.721) clearly beat PCA (0.599) and scGPT (0.507). ViT-L also beat ResNet50 under scVI (0.721 vs 0.688), though that rests on a single pair of runs. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder so far (0.72 vs 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion is slightly better than concat (0.725 vs 0.721) and cheaper (3.60 vs 4.65 GPU h). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. The RNA encoder has the biggest effect: scvi_n200 clearly beats pca_n2000, which clearly beats scgpt. imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50. Weighted fusion edges out concat, and transformer edges out avgpool, but both gaps are small. Every run so far has used multiprofile, so the profile setting is a completely untested design choice. 2. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder. That isolates the factor with the largest observed effect. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it settles the highest-impact open question before spending the remaining five runs on smaller choices such as fusion and aggregation. Expected cost is moderate, about 3.5-4.5 GPU hours, similar to config_050. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add slightly more cost than scVI's 200 dimensions.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.713 to 0.725, versus 0.586 for pca_n2000 and 0.520 for scgpt). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_050 (scVI_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy). The RNA encoder matters a lot: scVI clearly beats PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520). 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. With ViT-L, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion, scVI scored 0.725, PCA 0.586 and scGPT 0.520. 1. Evidence: Every multimodal multiprofile run so far points to scvi_n200 as the clearly best RNA encoder. Behind it are pca_n2000 (0.586) and scgpt (0.520). 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (about 0.71-0.72 vs 0.52 for scgpt and 0.59 for pca). 1. Evidence: scVI-200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, at 0.65 to 0.72 accuracy, versus 0.52 to 0.59 for scGPT and PCA. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_012 (scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.512 accuracy and 0.477 F1 at 4.33 GPU hours. 1) Evidence: with scGPT + ResNet50 + concat held fixed, avgpool aggregation (config_012, acc 0.512, F1 0.477) beat transformer aggregation (config_015, acc 0.471, F1 0.442) at about half the cost (4.33 vs 9.06 GPU hours). 1) Evidence so far: avgpool aggregation clearly beat transformer (0.512 vs 0.471), and the transformer cost about twice as much. 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reached 0.632 acc / 0.607 F1, and pca_n2000 reached 0.619, both far above scgpt at about 0.51. pca_n2000 also cost about 5x more than scvi (36.4 vs 7.3 GPU h). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_033 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion, 0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1). scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. The only transformer result (config_015, 0.471 vs 0.512 for avgpool) used the weak scGPT and ResNet50 pairing, so that single data point is weak evidence. 2. Test: config_051 changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation, keeping scVI, ViT-L and weighted fusion. This isolates whether learned aggregation helps once the encoders and fusion are strong. 3. Why now: it is the most direct remaining extension of the best configuration, and the result will guide the last two experiments. 1. Evidence: Every comparison so far favors weighted fusion over concat (+4.6 points with resnet50, +18.9 with ViT-L) and ViT-L over resnet50. Test: config_034 keeps the winning setup (ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for PCA-2000. Evidence: scVI-200 RNA embeddings with weighted fusion clearly lead this search. The best result is config_051 (scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.046 with scVI and ResNet50. Combining RNA and image usually beats either modality alone. Aggregating multiple profiles usually beats a single profile. Learned transformer aggregation may capture more than average pooling. 2. What this tests: config_044 is a strong anchor that combines these favoured choices: multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, scVI-200 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder and weighted fusion. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ViT-L images, avgpool, concat) reached 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1 at 4.54 GPU hours. This shows directly whether learned, attention-based pooling across profiles beats simple averaging. That is one of the most likely sources of a large accuracy gain in a multiprofile setup. 3) Why now: because only one factor changes, the result can be attributed cleanly. If it helps, later experiments can build on transformer aggregation while varying RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) and fusion type. If it does not, the cheaper avgpool stays as the default. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_043, roughly 1.2–1.5x (about 5.5–7 GPU hours), because of the transformer aggregator. Both accuracy and F1 agree, which suggests the simpler avgpool is at least as good here, though this is only a single comparison. The RNA encoder is still completely untested, and it is likely one of the highest-impact design choices. Test: config_047 keeps the best setup so far (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and swaps only PCA-2000 for the pretrained scGPT encoder. Expected cost is similar to config_043, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more if scGPT embeddings are larger. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.629 accuracy. Swapping in the scGPT RNA encoder cut accuracy by about 0.11, which was the largest effect seen. Transformer aggregation was about 0.03 worse than avgpool. So the RNA encoder looks like the most influential design choice, yet the third option, scvi_n200, is still untested. 2) This run keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200. 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder has the largest effect so far. scvi_n200 (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1) clearly beats pca_n2000 (0.629) and scgpt (0.518) with ViT-L, avgpool and concat. Evidence: the RNA encoder is the strongest factor so far. scVI (0.715) clearly beats PCA (0.629) and scGPT (0.518). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation with PCA (0.629 vs 0.599). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. 1) Evidence: scVI-n200 RNA and ImageNet ViT-L images are clearly the strongest choices. scVI beats PCA and scGPT by about 0.09 to 0.20 accuracy, and ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 0.08. 1. Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder with a multiprofile setup is clearly the strongest choice so far. What this tests: config_017 (RNA-only, scVI, transformer aggregation) checks an untested design choice, namely how much the image branch actually contributes, using the best RNA encoder and best aggregation. 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is open. In multimodal cellular profiling, the usual prior is that combining RNA and image data and aggregating across profiles improves accuracy, but that has not been tested here. 2) What this tests: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA, resnet50 image, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is a strong but not maximal-cost anchor. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI, ResNet50, transformer aggregation and concat fusion (config_030) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_002 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.721 accuracy. ViT-L beat ResNet50 under the same setup (0.688). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.72 vs 0.60 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT). ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). 1. Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. With the other settings fixed, scVI gave 0.72 accuracy, PCA 0.60 and scGPT 0.51. The image encoder mattered much less (ViT-L 0.72 vs ResNet50 0.69). Fusion and aggregation changes were also small: weighted fusion scored 0.725 vs 0.721 for concat, and the transformer scored 0.725 vs 0.706 for avgpool. 1) Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_027 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. Its close neighbours have mostly been tested. Concat fusion (0.721) and avgpool aggregation (0.706) were slightly worse. ResNet50 (0.688) and other RNA encoders (scGPT 0.507, PCA 0.599) were clearly worse, so switching encoders is unlikely to beat it. 2) Uncertainty: Profile setting is the one major design choice not yet tested; every multimodal run so far was multiprofile. Evidence: the best result is config_027 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc, F1 0.685). Its neighbours point the same way. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT. ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 0.033 under concat. Transformer beats avgpool by about 0.019 under weighted fusion. Weighted fusion is only marginally better than concat (about 0.004, within noise). Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin. Uncertainty: the one untested cell in the scVI + ViT-L multiprofile block is avgpool + concat. Because the fusion effect is small, it is unclear whether fusion and aggregation interact, for example whether concat pairs better with simple pooling. That tells us whether the transformer + weighted combination is truly the best or whether an interaction gives an upside. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 RNA is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (scgpt 0.507, pca 0.599). The only untested axis near the best region is the image encoder under weighted fusion: ResNet50 has been tried only with concat (config_030, 0.688). 2) This run tests whether weighted fusion closes the ResNet50 gap, completing the scvi/transformer/weighted cell of the design grid. 3) The alternatives look weaker. The large drops when scgpt or pca replace scvi suggest image features alone are not strong enough to beat 0.725, which argues against image-only runs. Configurations using pca or scgpt are dominated. config_028 is therefore the closest untested neighbor of the incumbent and the most plausible remaining chance of matching or exceeding it, though the expected gain is modest. For cellular profiling, the usual expectation is that combining RNA and image modalities and aggregating over multiple profiles beats single-modality, single-profile setups. Why now: Securing a strong baseline early guards the best-found accuracy within the 10-experiment budget and gives a clear reference for ablations. Why now: aggregation is a central design choice for every multiprofile configuration, so the answer shapes how the remaining 8 experiments are spent. The main design choice not yet tested is the profile setting: every run so far has been multiprofile. 2) This experiment keeps the best encoder and fusion choices (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) and switches to singleprofile, with no aggregation step. It tests whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed or whether a simpler per-profile model matches or beats it. 3) Expected cost is low, probably below config_034's 3.6 GPU hours, because there is no aggregation over multiple profiles. Its result will guide the final experiment: refine multiprofile further if singleprofile loses, or exploit the singleprofile direction if it wins.

1. Evidence: scVI-n200 RNA embeddings clearly beat PCA (0.57) and scGPT (0.49). Multiprofile transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706) and single-profile (0.537). The image encoder and fusion choices change accuracy only slightly: ViT-L weighted 0.725, ViT-L concat 0.721, ResNet50 weighted 0.713. These gaps are small enough to fall within run-to-run noise. 2. Test: this run tries the one remaining scVI + multiprofile + transformer combination, ResNet50 with concat fusion. It checks whether concat helps ResNet50 features enough to beat the current best (config_034, 0.725). It also tells us whether the image-encoder by fusion interaction matters. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: the other scVI untested options all use avgpool or single-profile, which were consistently worse. Image-only and alternative-RNA options are unlikely to beat the multimodal scVI setups. That makes this the last plausible winner within the strongest region found so far. Expected cost is moderate to high, about 5–6 GPU hours, similar to config_007 (6.22 h). That is more than the ViT-L runs (3.6–4.8 h) but far less than the scGPT run (12.3 h).

1. Evidence: The strong region is multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 with imagenet_vit_l. Within it, transformer aggregation scored 0.725 (config_034) and avgpool scored 0.706 (config_028), both with weighted fusion. Concat and weighted fusion scored about the same with ViT-L (0.721 vs 0.725). Moving away from this region hurt clearly: pca_n2000 scored 0.573, scgpt 0.494 and singleprofile 0.537. 2. What it tests: All transformer variants of this region are already done. config_020 is the last untested scvi_n200 + ViT-L multiprofile combination (avgpool aggregation, concat fusion). It checks whether concat fusion interacts better with avgpool than weighted fusion did. 3. Why it is the best final use: It stays in the best-performing region, so it has the best remaining chance of matching or slightly beating 0.725. Image-only, RNA-only, pca and scgpt options are much less likely to win, given the large drops seen when the RNA encoder or profile setting changed. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5 to 5 GPU hours, similar to config_019 and config_028.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multiple profiles, encoder type, aggregation or fusion. The working assumption is that combining RNA and image data and pooling over several profiles should give the most information, but this is untested. 2. What this tests: config_019 is a strong but moderately priced anchor. It combines both modalities and multiple profiles, using scVI-200 for RNA, ResNet50 for images, average pooling and concatenation fusion. It establishes a reference accuracy for the likely-best family, using the simpler and cheaper component at each choice: ResNet50 rather than ViT-L, average pooling rather than a transformer aggregator, and plain concatenation. Later runs can then change one factor at a time from this baseline. Examples are ViT-L, transformer aggregation, a different RNA encoder, weighted fusion, single-profile or single-modality versions. 3. Multiprofile and multimodal processing make it more expensive than single-profile or unimodal runs, but it should be clearly cheaper than ViT-L or transformer-aggregation configurations.

Evidence: only one result exists. config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1 at 7.27 GPU hours, so every design factor is still uncertain. Test: config_023 changes one thing, avgpool to transformer aggregation, keeping everything else fixed. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging. Aggregation is a core design choice for multiprofile models and could give a large gain. Why now: a one-factor change lets me read the effect cleanly against the only baseline. Testing aggregation first is cheaper than swapping in ViT-L, and whichever aggregator wins can then be carried into the encoder and fusion comparisons. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_019 because of the transformer aggregator, roughly 8 to 10 GPU hours, but well below a ViT-L multiprofile run.

1) Evidence: The best so far is config_041 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Three choices are fairly settled. Transformer beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632). 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_041 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. 1. Evidence: we have only one result so far. config_013 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.688 validation accuracy and 0.659 F1. 1) Evidence: Two experiments so far share scVI RNA encoding, multiprofile transformer aggregation and concat fusion. Swapping the ResNet50 image encoder for ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.688 to 0.721, and F1 rose with it (0.659 to 0.681). ViT-L was also slightly cheaper (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU hours). Fusion type (config_031) and avgpool aggregation (config_033) can be tested afterward on the winning RNA encoder. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is 0.721 accuracy (F1 0.681). It came from scVI RNA with ViT-L images, a transformer aggregator and concat fusion, using multimodal multiprofile inputs. The RNA encoder is clearly the dominant factor. Swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L gained about 3 points. The third RNA encoder, PCA-2000, is still completely untested. 2) Test: config_007 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder to PCA-2000. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. Expected cost is similar to config_003, about 4.5-5 GPU hours. Weighted fusion matches or slightly beats concat (0.725 vs 0.721) and costs less (3.6 vs 4.65 GPU h). 1) Evidence: config_031 is the current best at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1, using scVI, ViT-L, a transformer aggregator and weighted fusion. Adding the two observed drops predicts about 0.70 for config_014 (ResNet50, weighted) is weaker, at roughly 0.69 by the same additive estimate. PCA, scGPT and single-profile options are much weaker. It is multimodal and multiprofile with transformer aggregation, which usually gives the highest accuracy when aggregating cell profiles. Later experiments can then vary one factor at a time from this baseline: avgpool vs transformer, weighted vs concat, scGPT/scVI vs PCA, ViT-L vs ResNet50, and single-profile or unimodal ablations. 3) Starting from a likely high-performing but moderately priced setup gives a competitive early best score while keeping GPU hours down. It also anchors the comparisons for the remaining 9 experiments. Expected relative cost is medium: multiprofile transformer aggregation with multimodal inputs costs more than single-profile or unimodal runs, but less than variants using ViT-L or scGPT.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. Config_044 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 images, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.579 accuracy and 0.563 F1 for 6.76 GPU hours. A single point says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_002 is a one-factor change that swaps the PCA RNA encoder for the pretrained scGPT foundation-model embedding and keeps everything else fixed. Any accuracy or F1 difference can therefore be attributed to the RNA representation. This is likely one of the most influential choices, and it determines which encoder to carry forward in later combinations with ViT-L images, avgpool aggregation or weighted fusion. 3) Why now: the result points directly at the more promising RNA encoder while keeping the strong multiprofile-transformer backbone. With 8 experiments left, establishing the RNA encoder first lets later runs build on the stronger choice. Expected cost is similar to or slightly above config_044 (about 7 to 8 GPU hours), because scGPT embeddings are larger than PCA features but the rest of the architecture is unchanged.

1) Evidence: with resnet50, transformer aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, pca_n2000 RNA beat scgpt by about 11 points in accuracy (0.579 vs 0.471), and F1 showed the same gap. That makes pca_n2000 the current anchor. The image encoder is the other major untested axis and could have a similarly large effect. 2) This experiment changes one factor from the best configuration, config_044, swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. Whichever image encoder wins can then serve as the base for cheaper refinements such as weighted fusion or avgpool aggregation. 1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest factor seen so far. With the same resnet50, transformer and concat setup, pca_n2000 reached 0.579 accuracy versus 0.471 for scGPT, a gap of about 0.11. Swapping the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l gave a smaller gain, to 0.599 accuracy and 0.578 F1 (config_042, the current best). The third RNA encoder, scvi_n200, has never been tested. 2. Test: config_007 keeps config_042's best setup (vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200. This is a clean one-variable comparison of RNA encoders on the strongest backbone. 3. Why now: the RNA encoder has shown the largest effect, so leaving scVI untested is the biggest remaining uncertainty that could change the overall best. Fusion type (weighted) and aggregation (avgpool) are likely smaller refinements that can be tested in later experiments on whichever RNA encoder wins. That makes it cheaper than the resnet50 and scGPT runs (6.76 and 9.06 GPU hours).

1) Evidence: The strongest signal so far is the RNA encoder. scVI (config_007, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1) clearly beats PCA (0.599) and scGPT (0.471) when combined with ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. ViT-L also slightly beats ResNet50 and is cheaper (about 4.7 vs 6.8 GPU h).
