Evidence: scvi_n200 RNA paired with the imagenet_vit_l image encoder is clearly the strongest combination so far. Transformer and avgpool aggregation scored about the same (0.721 vs 0.715 accuracy), and avgpool had slightly higher F1 (0.687 vs 0.681) at lower cost (4.49 vs 4.65 GPU hours). Fusion is the main design choice still untested: every run so far used concat. Test: config_019 keeps the best scvi_n200 + ViT-L multiprofile setup with the cheaper avgpool aggregation and switches fusion to weighted. This isolates whether weighted fusion can push past about 0.72. Why now: it exploits the best-performing region while settling an open design question, which leaves 3 runs to follow up (e.g., weighted fusion with transformer aggregation if it helps). Expected cost is low, similar to config_034 at roughly 4.5 GPU hours, and among the cheapest multimodal multiprofile options.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reaches 0.706-0.721, while pca_n2000 is about 0.58-0.60 and scgpt is 0.47. imagenet_vit_l beat resnet50 under pca (0.599 vs 0.579) and was cheaper. With scvi plus ViT-L, transformer and avgpool aggregation give nearly the same result (0.721 vs 0.715). Weighted fusion was slightly below concat with avgpool (0.706 vs 0.715), but that is a single, small difference. 2) This experiment: It tests weighted fusion with transformer aggregation on the current best backbone (scvi_n200 + ViT-L). It is the last untested one-factor variant of the top configuration that keeps both of the strongest encoders. It shows whether learned modality weighting interacts with transformer aggregation to beat 0.721, or confirms that concat is the better fusion choice. 3) Why now: Weaker encoders, single-profile and unimodal options look unlikely to beat 0.72. Exploiting the best region is therefore the most promising use of the remaining budget. Expected cost is moderate and similar to config_007, about 4.7-5 GPU hours.

Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. With ViT-L, moving from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 raised accuracy from about 0.60 to about 0.72. All four aggregation and fusion combinations of scvi_n200 + ViT-L multiprofile are now tested and fall within a narrow 0.706–0.725 band (F1 0.667–0.687), so that local neighborhood is largely exhausted. ViT-L beat ResNet50 for PCA (0.599 vs 0.579), so swapping in ResNet50 with scVI is unlikely to raise the best result. The main untested question is how much the image modality actually contributes, given how strongly RNA drives performance. This experiment runs scvi_n200 RNA-only with transformer aggregation, matching the best setup without the image branch. If it matches or beats 0.725, that is a direct gain. If it is clearly worse, it confirms that the multimodal design matters, and I can use the last experiment on a refinement near the current best. Expected cost is lower than the multimodal runs (roughly 2–3 GPU hours versus 3.6–4.8), since there is no image encoder or fusion.

Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. scVI runs scored 0.706-0.725, versus about 0.58-0.60 for PCA and 0.47 for scGPT. The scVI + ViT-L multiprofile grid is now complete (aggregation x fusion), and its four results fall within about 0.02 of each other. The best is config_014 (transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc), so more aggregation or fusion tweaks with ViT-L offer little upside. The image encoder is the main design choice not yet tested with scVI. With PCA, ResNet50 trailed ViT-L by only about 0.02, a gap small enough that it may not carry over to the stronger RNA encoder. This experiment pairs scVI with ResNet50 using the best-performing transformer + weighted setup. It tests whether a different image representation complements scVI better. It is the only remaining multiprofile multimodal direction with a realistic chance of beating 0.725; single-profile and scGPT options look clearly weaker from current evidence. Expected cost is moderate to high. Past ResNet50 multiprofile runs took about 6.8-9 GPU hours, above the 3.6-4.8 hours of the ViT-L runs. This is acceptable because it addresses the last important open axis, and the final experiment can then exploit whichever image encoder wins.

1. Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. Its multimodal multiprofile runs scored 0.706-0.725, compared with 0.47-0.60 for pca and scgpt and 0.653 for RNA-only. The current best is config_014 (scvi + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725). Aggregation and fusion choices differ by only about 1-2 points, so they are within noise. The scvi + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted run (config_032) reached 0.713 accuracy with the highest F1 seen so far (0.695), which suggests ResNet50 pairs well with scvi. 2. Test: config_016 completes the scvi/ResNet50/transformer pairing with concat fusion. Concat matched weighted fusion on the ViT-L transformer runs (0.721 vs 0.725) and slightly beat it under avgpool (0.715 vs 0.706). This gives another realistic shot at a new best within the strongest region of the search space. 3. Why it is the best final use: with no budget left, exploiting the proven scvi multimodal multiprofile region is the most likely route to beating 0.725. Untested single-profile variants are cheaper but unlikely to beat multiprofile aggregation. Expected cost is moderately high, about 6-6.5 GPU hours, similar to config_032 because of the ResNet50 multiprofile transformer pipeline.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so I am relying on priors. The design choices most likely to drive accuracy are multimodal versus unimodal input and multiprofile versus single-profile input. Combining RNA and imaging data across several profiles, with learned transformer aggregation, is the most plausible high-accuracy region. 2. What this tests: config_001 combines multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA embeddings, a ResNet50 image encoder, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. It is a strong mid-cost anchor in that region. Later runs can each change one factor from it: avgpool versus transformer, weighted versus concat fusion, ViT-L versus ResNet50, or unimodal and single-profile ablations. 3. Why now: it targets the likely best region without starting with the most expensive ViT-L combinations. That gives an early high baseline while leaving budget for one-factor comparisons. The compact scVI and ResNet50 encoders keep it cheaper than the ViT-L or scGPT variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: we have only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile baseline (scVI-200 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1 at 5.16 GPU hours. With a single data point, every design choice is still uncertain. The image encoder is probably among the highest-impact choices, since ImageNet ViT-L gives much richer representations than ResNet50. 2. What this tests: config_049 changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L and keeps everything else identical. Any change in accuracy can therefore be attributed to the image encoder. The result will tell us which backbone to carry into later multimodal experiments. 3. Why now: this is the clearest single-factor test of an important choice, and it also has the most likely upside for raising the best accuracy. Cheaper ablations such as avgpool, RNA-only or a different RNA encoder can follow once we know which image backbone to use. Expected cost is about 1.5–2x config_001, roughly 8–10 GPU hours, because ViT-L features are larger and multiprofile transformer aggregation adds cost. That is justified because this configuration is a strong candidate for the best performer.

Evidence: the two runs differ only in image encoder. ImageNet ViT-L beat ResNet50 (val acc 0.721 vs 0.688, F1 0.681 vs 0.659) and was also slightly cheaper (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU hours). This is a single comparison, but it is enough to keep ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation and concat fusion as the working base. The RNA encoder is the largest untested design choice so far, since only scVI has been tried. This experiment swaps scVI for the scGPT foundation-model embedding and keeps everything else fixed, so any change can be attributed to the RNA encoder. That is the best use of the next run because it tests a high-impact axis with clear upside while building on the best configuration found so far. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_049 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3 points. The RNA encoder had by far the largest effect: swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507. The third RNA option, PCA (2,000 components), is completely untested, so the RNA encoder is the largest remaining uncertainty. 2) Test: config_010 keeps config_049's setup and changes only the RNA encoder to PCA. This isolates whether PCA matches or beats scVI. 3) Why now: because the RNA encoder shifts accuracy so much, settling it first gives the most information and the best chance of a new top score. Fusion (weighted vs concat) and aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) can be refined afterwards on the winning encoder. Expected cost is similar to config_049, roughly 4.5–5 GPU hours (multiprofile, multimodal, transformer). PCA features may make it slightly cheaper than scVI, which is attractive at similar or better accuracy.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder matters a lot. With ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, scVI reached 0.721 accuracy, PCA 0.599 and scGPT 0.507. Swapping to ResNet50 with scVI gave 0.688, so ViT-L looks better, and its run was no more expensive. Fusion and aggregation have not been varied at all: every run so far used transformer aggregation with concat fusion. 2) This run keeps the best setup (scVI + ViT-L + transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. It isolates whether learned modality weighting improves on plain concatenation. That is plausible here because the two modalities differ clearly in quality, as the large encoder-dependent swings suggest. 3) Fusion is the most important untested design choice around the current best, so this is the right balance between exploiting the best setup and resolving a key uncertainty. Weighted fusion adds negligible overhead.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder. It reached 0.72 with ViT-L, versus 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt. ViT-L beats resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688 with concat). Weighted fusion is marginally better than concat (0.725 vs 0.721, F1 0.685 vs 0.681) and was cheaper (3.60 vs 4.65 GPU hours). Aggregation is the main untested design choice: every run so far used the transformer. 2) Test: config_012 keeps the best setup (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + weighted fusion) and swaps the transformer for avgpool. This shows whether the transformer adds accuracy or whether simple pooling matches or beats it. 3) Why now: it exploits the best-known components while resolving a key uncertainty, and the result will guide the last 4 experiments (e.g., whether to test singleprofile next). 1) Evidence: every experiment so far has been multiprofile. Within that setting the best configuration is clear: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_017, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). The RNA encoder matters a lot: scvi is far ahead of pca and scgpt. ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer slightly beats avgpool, and weighted fusion is marginally better than concat. The profile setting is the one major design axis that has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best encoder and fusion choices fixed and switches to single-profile (no aggregation). That isolates how much multiprofile aggregation actually contributes. 3) Remaining gains from the encoder, aggregation and fusion axes look small and are largely settled. Testing the untested profile axis reduces the most uncertainty about whether a better region exists. It is also likely the cheapest run so far, because no multiprofile aggregation is needed (well below the ~3.6–5 GPU hours of the multiprofile runs). If it underperforms, it confirms multiprofile, and the last two experiments can go to refinements such as unimodal ablations.

1) Evidence: The best result is config_017 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Each tested axis favours the choices it already uses. The RNA encoder matters most: scVI scored 0.72, PCA 0.60 and scGPT 0.51. Image encoder (ViT-L over ResNet50), aggregation (transformer over avgpool) and fusion (weighted over concat) give smaller gains of 0.004 to 0.033. Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. So the remaining multimodal scVI variants (config_026, 043, 013, 045) each swap in a choice that was weaker, and are predicted to land below 0.725. 2) Uncertainty: The large RNA-encoder sensitivity suggests performance is driven mainly by the RNA representation, but no unimodal baseline has been tested. This experiment tests whether scVI RNA-only with transformer aggregation is competitive with, or better than, the multimodal model. That would show whether the image branch adds signal or noise, and would inform the final experiment, either a unimodal refinement or a final multimodal check. 3) Why now: It is the highest-uncertainty experiment that could still produce a new best, unlike the predictable multimodal variants. With 2 runs left, it also leaves one run for exploitation. Expected cost is lower than the multimodal multiprofile runs (about 2 to 3.5 GPU hours versus 3.6 to 5.2) because there is no ViT-L image branch.

1) Evidence: the best result is config_017 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The nearby variants all scored lower. Concat fusion gave 0.721, avgpool gave 0.706 and ResNet50 gave 0.688. The scGPT (0.507) and PCA (0.599) RNA encoders were much worse, and single-profile was much worse (0.537). So the remaining untested neighbours of config_017 (config_043 avgpool+concat, config_026 ResNet50+weighted, config_027 PCA) are each expected to fall below it. 2) Open question: the main untested design choice is whether the ViT-L image modality alone, with transformer aggregation, matches or beats fusion. RNA-only reached 0.653, and a weak RNA encoder clearly dragged multimodal models down, so RNA may add noise as well as signal. This experiment measures how much image-only contributes. 3) Why now: of the remaining options, it has the highest outcome variance and a plausible chance of exceeding 0.725. It also tells the final experiment whether to keep RNA. Expected cost is moderate, about 2-3 GPU hours, cheaper than multimodal multiprofile runs (3.6-5.2 h) because no RNA branch or fusion is trained.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (scGPT 0.507, PCA 0.599). ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 0.033 under concat fusion. Transformer beats avgpool by about 0.019 under weighted fusion. Weighted and concat fusion are nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721). Multiprofile and multimodal settings are essential. Every high-value direction near the top has been tested except a few scVI multimodal variants.

2. What this tests: config_043 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat) is the remaining untested combination closest to the best configuration. It changes only the cheaper avgpool aggregation and keeps the stronger ViT-L image encoder. Because fusion choice made little difference, its expected accuracy (~0.70) is above the ResNet50 alternative config_026 (~0.69). It also checks whether avgpool's penalty depends on fusion type.

3. Why it is the best final pick: Beating 0.725 is unlikely with any remaining option, but config_043 has the highest expected accuracy among them and so the best chance of a new maximum through run-to-run variance. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_012.
